title: Philo Sets Exclusive Streaming Date for Page Six ‘Virtual Reali-Tea Awards’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tim Chan Plus Icon Tim Chan @mrtimchan Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 7:00am Reality stars attend the 2025 Page Six Virtual Reali-Tea Awards at City Winery on September 17, 2025 in New York City Manny Carabel/Getty Images If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, The Hollywood Reporter may receive an affiliate commission. Live TV streamer Philo has landed Page Six ‘s “Virtual Reali-Tea Awards,” the New York Post Media Group’s fan-voted awards show that celebrates reality television. This year’s Virtual Reali-Tea Awards ceremony films on Oct. 6 at New York’s Edison Ballroom and will premiere exclusively on Philo beginning on Oct. 9. Worth noting: while Philo subscribers can currently enjoy 70+ live TV channels and thousands of on-demand shows and movies for a $25 monthly price point , this year’s awards show will stream free for everyone — no subscription required. Related Stories TV 'Real Housewives of Rhode Island' Star Alicia Carmody on How the Bravo Series Changed Her Life: "I Never Knew I Could Work This Hard" TV Kim Kardashian Debuts New Reality Show 'Team Moms: Baseball': Where to Watch Online STREAM VIRTUAL REALI-TEA AWARDS ON PHILO Last year’s Virtual Reali-Tea Awards featured cast members from Bravo’s The Real Housewives of Miami, The Real Housewives of New Jersey, Southern Hospitality and MTV’s Teen Mom , among others. According to a press release, this year’s show will feature appearances by reality stars like Real Housewives of New York’s Countess Luann de Lesseps, Kyle Cooke from Summer House , The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Layla Taylor, and Jersey Shore star Mike “The Situation” Sorrentino, among others. De Lesseps, of course, is now part of the cast for E!’s The Golden Life , which was pitched as a Real Housewives of New York reboot. She’ll be joined by her current castmates (and former RHONY stars) Sonja Morgan, Ramona Singer, Dorinda Medley and Kelly Bensimon to accept the coveted Golden Kettle Lifetime Achievement Award. The Countess is also slated to perform at the event, with other musical acts that include Real Housewives of Potomac star Ashley Darby and Vanderpump Rules alum Scheana Shay. All three are also nominated in the Musician of the Year category, alongside Atlanta housewife, Drew Sidora. Other categories include Quote of the Year, “Hot-Tea of the Year,” Best Reunion Performance and Best Return to Screen. Philo will sponsor the Best Cast category with the stars of Jersey Shore Family Reunion, Real Housewives of Rhode Island, Traitors and Love Thy Nader making up the nominees. The Virtual Reali-Tea awards show is a spin-off of Page Six’s popular pop culture and reality TV podcast of the same name, and this year’s ceremony will be hosted and executive produced by the podcast hosts, Danny Murphy and Evan Real. The awards are also Philo’s first exclusively licensed original show in the awards category, and continues the streamer’s push into original programming. “Philo is known for being a home for reality TV lovers,” says Mike Keyserling, CEO of Philo, in a release. “We’re proud to be the exclusive streaming home of the Virtual Reali-Tea Awards and to give reality TV fans on our platform even more of what they enjoy.” “Reality TV is a huge part of the Page Six universe, and the Virtual Reali-Tea Awards have quickly become a standout extension of the brand,” adds Sean Giancola, Publisher and CEO of New York Post Media Group. “Philo is a natural partner to help us take the VRT Awards to the next level, reach even more fans and celebrate the people and moments everyone is talking about.” Philo currently offers more than 70 live television channels that subscribers can stream online without cable, including shows and movies on AMC, ID and Lifetime, plus popular reality series on MTV, TLC, VH1 and We TV. Philo plans start at just $25/month . SEE LATEST PHILO STREAMING OFFERS Philo also offers a free tier that gives viewers access to more than 150 free, ad-supported channels along with thousands of movies and shows on demand — no credit card or signup required. The Virtual Reali-Tea Awards will debut as part of Philo’s free channel lineup. Tune into the exclusive streaming premiere of the 2026 Virtual Reali-Tea Awards on October 9 and catch up on last year’s awards at Philo.com/VRTs . THR

full_text: Sep 24, 2026 7:00am PT Tribeca Festival Opens Submissions for Untold Stories Filmmaker Program With $1.2 Million Prize (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest The Best Pop Culture Halloween Costumes for 2026: From Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Shrubs to Taylor Swift’s Knicks Shirt 16 hours ago Los Angeles Lakers Release Official Photo Book Chronicling Seven Decades of Purple-and-Gold History 18 hours ago No, Those Dior x A24 Shirts Aren’t Going on Sale 18 hours ago See All Tribeca Festival and AT&T have opened submissions for the 10th anniversary of AT&T Untold Stories, the filmmaker development program that awards one emerging director $1.2 million to produce a feature film. The production prize, which increased from $1 million to $1.2 million in 2026, is billed by Tribeca and AT&T as the largest unrestricted film production award of its kind in the world. Submissions for the upcoming edition are open through Jan. 18. Related Stories Paranormal Comedy 'Don't F — k With Ghosts' Premieres On Demand, Launches Original YouTube Channel (EXCLUSIVE) Netflix, Amazon and YouTube Form D.C. Lobbying Group Amid Backlash Over Cost of Sports on Streaming Each year, five filmmaking teams are selected to pitch their projects live at the Tribeca Festival, with one winner receiving full production funding, year-round mentorship and support from Tribeca Studios. The winning film is also guaranteed a premiere at the following year’s festival. Popular on Variety The next recipient will be selected at the 2027 Tribeca Festival and will receive $1.2 million toward production ahead of a guaranteed premiere at the 2028 edition. “Tribeca is incredibly proud of our decade-long collaboration with AT&T and the success of the filmmakers who have come through Untold Stories,” said Bryce Norbitz, VP of Tribeca Studios and artist development. “We’ve watched pioneering storytellers take bold new ideas from concept to screen, garner the support of major distributors, and reach the audiences their stories deserve.” Norbitz added that the program’s continued growth is “a testament to the power of investing in emerging voices, especially at a time when independent filmmaking has never been tougher.” Launched in 2017, Untold Stories has awarded more than $9.2 million in funding, supported more than 45 projects and produced eight feature films. Recent winners include David Fortune’s “Color Book,” Lilian T. Mehrel’s “Honeyjoon” and Liz Sargent’s “Take Me Home,” all of which secured theatrical releases in 2026. Other past recipients include Faraday Okoro’s “Nigerian Prince,” Sasie Sealy’s “Lucky Grandma,” Kate Tsang’s “Marvelous and the Black Hole,” Nardeep Khurmi’s “Land of Gold,” So Young Shelly Yo’s “Smoking Tigers” and Sid Gopinath’s 2026 winner “Minnesota Goodbye.” Filmmakers can submit projects through Jan. 18 at Tribeca’s Untold Stories website. title: CNN, MS NOW And Politico Say White House Continues To Deny Access To Some Staffers Even After Judge’s Order
full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked By Judge, Who Orders CNN, Politico & MS NOW Credentials Restored Judge Says He’ll Rule “As Soon As I Can” On Trump’s Ban On CNN, Politico And MS NOW; Expresses Concern Over Due Process CNN CEO Mark Thompson Addresses Donald Trump’s White House Ban, Pending Paramount Merger In Town Hall View All September 24, 2026 6:54am Donald Trump Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images The White House has continued to deny access to reporters for CNN , Politico and MS NOW , even after a judge ruled against Donald Trump ‘s ban and that credentials must be restored. CNN’s Betsy Klein reported that she was still not being allowed access to the grounds, and did a standup from outside the White House gates. Politico reported that one of its correspondents was turned away and his press credentials were confiscated. MS NOW reporter Laura Barrón-López and a producer were denied access and had their passes confiscated, the network reported. Related Stories News Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked By Judge, Who Orders CNN, Politico & MS NOW Credentials Restored News Reporters Committee And Dozens Of Media Outlets File Legal Brief Urging Judge To End Trump’s Ban On CNN, Politico And MS Now U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, in a ruling issued overnight, issued a temporary restraining order that requires that access be restored. He concluded that the outlets were denied due process, but also indicated that the media plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their Fifth Amendment claims. The order lasts for 14 days as he considers further legal arguments. As of Thursday morning, there was still no TV pool to cover the president and first lady’s ceremony to greet Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan. After CNN was removed from its pool assignment on Monday, the other four networks in the TV pool announced that they would not participate in the rotation. He wrote that “time is of the essence —CNN is scheduled to be the television pool this evening for President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House.” “Defendants have already repeatedly violated the court’s order,” Boutrous wrote. title: ECAM Incubator Title ‘Copy’ Pairs a Heartbroken Film Assistant With a Movie Star Accused of Murder
full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:53am PT ECAM Incubator Title ‘Copy’ Pairs a Heartbroken Film Assistant With a Movie Star Accused of Murder By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest ‘Suro’ Director Mikel Gurrea on ‘Saints,’ Directing ‘The Beloved’ Star Victoria Luengo, Religious-Art Theft and Finding Mystery in Care 5 hours ago ‘200 Lives, Paco Rabal,’ Told in the Spanish Screen Legend’s Own Voice, Boarded by Latido Films 5 hours ago Juan Sebastián Mesa, Tatiana Huezo, Felipe Solari Yrigoyen Triumph at San Sebastián Industry Awards 19 hours ago See All Ángeles L. Guerrero, Miguel Machetti and Tina V. Mollá Courtesy of Gelatina Películas What happens when an emotionally stranded young film worker becomes indispensable to one of the world’s biggest stars who may also be a murderer? That collision drives “Copy” (“El participio del verbo oír”), Miguel Machetti’s feature project, currently in development and produced by Ángeles L. Guerrero and Tina V. Mollá through Gelatina Películas . Selected for the ninth edition of Madrid film school ECAM’s prestigious Incubator, the project was also presented in ECAM Forum’s 2026 Films to Come strand. Related Stories Paranormal Comedy 'Don't F — k With Ghosts' Premieres On Demand, Launches Original YouTube Channel (EXCLUSIVE) Emmys in Talks to Move to Amazon Prime Video Under New Licensing Arrangement, as the Broadcast Wheel Deal Ends (EXCLUSIVE) The story follows Ramón, a film assistant reeling from a painful breakup, who begins working with Camille de Valois, a legendary French actress returning to cinema after two decades away following an accusation of murder. Popular on Variety “One of the most important themes to explore throughout the film was always the extraordinary within the absolute normality of everyday life,” Machetti told Variety. “Everyone has perhaps experienced a painful breakup, but what would it be like to face one alongside a living legend and potential serial killer?” While everyone around Ramón obsesses over whether Camille actually committed the crime, Ramón becomes far more consumed by the attention she gives him. “The fact that the most famous person in the world sees him, recognises him and, in many cases, depends on him, makes everything else fade into the background,” Machetti said. That dependency also attracted Gelatina to the project. Founded in 2025 by Guerrero and Mollá, the young company see in “Copy” both an unconventional first feature and a story they hope will travel beyond its film-industry setting. “You do not have to work for a major film star to recognise yourself in a toxic relationship from which you feel unable to escape,” the producers said. “Beneath its specific setting, ‘Copy’ speaks to something far more universal: the power dynamics, dependencies and contradictions that can shape our relationships with others and with ourselves.” Those power imbalances extend to the film set. Machetti drew on years working in assistant direction, describing the industry as “an extremely hierarchical environment.” The project is now entering its final stages of development, according to Gelatina, with international co-production a priority. The producers are particularly looking toward France and Belgium and envision Camille being played by an established French or Italian actress opposite a largely unknown actor as Ramón. “This echoes the central dynamic of the film itself: a young outsider suddenly sharing the screen with an established star,” they said. “The casting becomes an extension of the story, allowing fiction and reality to subtly mirror one another.” Filmmakers out of the incubator have included Jaione Camborda (“The Rye Horn”), Estibaliz Urresola (“20,000 Species of Bees,”) and Alauda Ruiz de Azúa (“Lullaby,” “Sundays.”) For Machetti, even the title crystallizes the hierarchy. “Copy” is Ramón’s habitual radio response. “It is perhaps the word he says most often throughout the day,” he said, “through a device that seems like an extension of his own body, and through which he only receives orders that he has to carry out.” SND Swoops on Toronto-Bound Bérénice Bejo Starrer ‘Alice: Pioneer of Cinema’ Ahead of Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Kill Jackie,’ Starring a Glamorous, Lethal Catherine Zeta-Jones, Acquired by Warner Bros. title: Zurich Film Festival Heads on Theatrical-Loving Gen Z, Prioritizing Private Equity and Tilly Norwood a Year Later: This Is the ‘Place Where You Address the Real Hot Questions’
full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:52am PT Zurich Film Festival Heads on Theatrical-Loving Gen Z, Prioritizing Private Equity and Tilly Norwood a Year Later: This Is the ‘Place Where You Address the Real Hot Questions’ The festival will also continue to cement its reputation as an awards launchpad with screenings of titles such as 'I Play Rocky,' 'Wild Horse Nine,' 'Tenzing' and 'The Debut' By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Brazil’s Desvia Filmes Enters New Era With Doubled Focus on Indie and Rachel Daisy Ellis’ San Sebastián Co-Pro Forum’s Buzzy ‘The Last Cruise’ 48 minutes ago Mauro Mueller’s ‘111 – Echoes From Halifax’ Might Chronicle Tragic 1998 Swissair Plane Crash, but This Is Not Your Regular Disaster Movie 1 hour ago San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference: 10 Takeaways From AI to ‘Obsession,’ YouTube and Why International Movies Could Dominate the Oscars 5 hours ago See All Courtesy of Zurich Film Festival If one film could define this year’s Zurich Film Festival , it would be Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” a heartfelt drama about the making of the Sylvester Stallone-starring classic that is playing as one of the festival galas. The film embodies not only the festival’s 2026 motto of “Dream Big,” but also a go-getter attitude that saw CEO Christian Jungen buy out former owner — Swiss newspaper NZZ — and lead the festival alongside an investment team that secured private funds to ensure the event’s continuity and independence. A year on from the bold strategic move, Jungen is confident in its success and the advantages it brings for the future. Related Stories Amazon's Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors' Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series 'Maxton Hall' Emmys in Talks to Move to Amazon Prime Video Under New Licensing Arrangement, as the Broadcast Wheel Deal Ends (EXCLUSIVE) Speaking with Variety ahead of this year’s edition from an office decorated from wall to wall with prized “Rocky” collector items — think golden gloves, intricate statues and vintage posters — Jungen says the Farrelly film has been a great source of inspiration for this year’s festival. “It’s a film about a big dream. In these rough times, when it’s very tough to finance films, that’s something that is going to speak to everybody in the industry. I am sure it will be embraced broadly in our industry and with audiences. It’s a crowdpleaser.” Popular on Variety Jungen says delivering the festival is now “easier because we are independent.” “In these polarized times, we got caught up in political discussions,” he adds, referring to the NZZ’s right-wing-leaning editorial line. “Now it’s all about cinema again. Not that it wasn’t before, of course, but when you belong to a newspaper, and they have strong opinions, you risk becoming collateral damage.” “We found new partners for the first time in five years, which is good because it’s very challenging to finance cultural events,” he went on. “Most partners want to be part of emotional stories. It’s more about telling stories together than about visibility. Ten years ago, they paid money, and you put their logo on the photo wall. Today, they want to offer their employees or clients an emotional evening, and are very interested in having talent on stage. That doesn’t mean just big Hollywood stars.” But it is indeed a starry roster, with the likes of Martin McDonagh, Anna Kendrick, Jesse Eisenberg, Tom Hiddleston and Naomi Watts all landing in the Swiss city over the next few days. The festival, which kicks off with the European premiere of the Hiddleston-starring “Tenzing,” will host European premieres of several other major fall festival titles, including Chris Rock’s “Misty Green,” Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” and Lauren Miller Rogen’s “Babies,” starring Kendrick and Seth Rogen. Other major titles such as “Bunker,” “Ink,” “Club Kid,” “The Debut” and “Wild Horse Nine” will also bow at the festival. Jungen remains focused on making Zurich a strong awards launchpad. “After the first premiere, films need a second turf to display their stars and start a conversation,” he says. “The good thing abut Zurich is you have a film-friendly audience and, at the same time, we are the door to the German-speaking world, which is a $100 million market. We are a real test with audiences, and our positioning is glamorous. For us, it’s important to be a platform with a real audience, but also to have an impact with Academy or Golden Globe voters.” “We are at the end of fall festival season, and many of the decision-makers from the industry who were in Venice went over to Toronto and are maybe doing San Sebastián, and have Zurich as their last stop, where they finally have time to watch a movie,” he notes. “It just so happened that, over the last years, films that had their European premiere in Zurich, whether it was ‘Green Book’ or ‘All Quiet on the Western Front,’ were successful at the Oscars. This could be the case for ‘I Play Rocky’ or ‘Tenzing.’” “I Play Rocky,” courtesy of Zurich Film Festival Zurich is also a great city for theatrical exhibition, featuring 63 movie theaters for a population of 440,000, making it one of the strongest exhibition capitals in the world. And the festival has a young audience eager to fill those seats. “Gen Z is reawakening cinema,” says festival director and co-owner Reta Guetg. “That is really cool, and I think only the start of a wave that will keep growing. Our young programming team was raving about Rhys Marc Jones’s ‘Black Church Bay,’ a thriller starring Joe Locke, who is also one of our guests. The film is a world premiere; it has amazing direction, really interesting cast. These kinds of films help shape the program. We try to be at the forefront of discovering new talent.” This interest in new talent doesn’t come only from audiences, but it is also shared by the high-profile executives travelling into town for the festival’s highly prestigious industry sidebar, the Zurich Summit . “They are always asking me: who are the creatives this year? Who is the up-and-coming talent? What should we see? They are actually more interested than you would think in new talent,” says Guetg. “We have a panel this year with the CEO of the Oscars, Bill Kramer, who will sit next to [‘Obsession’ director] Kane Parsons, a 20-year-old still living with his parents in San Francisco, and a sensation who cracked 4 million admissions in cinemas,” she adds. “And they are both eager to hear from each other. It’s a great space to make these connections happen because we have a lot of openness from both sides.” A year ago, the Summit made major headlines when it introduced the market to AI-generated actress Tilly Norwood, launched by AI talent studio Xicoia. Asked about Norwood’s impact — and controversies — in the year since, Jungen says, “Zurich is the place where you address the real hot questions.” Tilly Norwood, courtesy of Xicoia Courtesy of Particle6 “AI is the big game changer of our times,” he goes on. “In my mind, it’s bigger than the introduction of the internet in the late 90s. We didn’t expect the reactions to Tilly Norwood last year, but it proves there is a lot of energy in those questions. The Zurich Summit takes place in neutral Switzerland; it’s where everybody finds common ground, where Americans meet Europeans. We have a tradition of being a platform for exchange and openness.” The festival will also bring back the Film Finance Forum, an event even more exclusive than the already exclusive Summit. The Forum takes place a day before the conference and brings together bankers, investors and major producers for closed-door discussions on film financing. “We want to put our international guests in an exchange with the people from the finance industry here,” says Jungen. “Quite a few companies have found investors for their businesses at the Zurich Summit, and that’s a role we want to play. We want to turn Zurich into a platform where you get access to private equity because this is the way to go, as the pre-sale business is truly challenging.” “With private equity, we can move faster, produce faster, and since Zurich is literally the world capital of wealth management boutiques, I think we have a lot of stakeholders who might be interested in hearing from the lion’s mouth, from people from Los Angeles or New York who can say that investing in film can mean a return,” says the festival head. “Investing in film — it’s not just about supporting the arts; it’s business.” The Zurich Film Festival runs Sept. 24-Oct. 4. title: YouTube Bets That a Slew of AI-Powered Features Can Maintain Its Video Domination
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 6:50am YouTube Custom Feeds YouTube YouTube may be the most-watched video platform on planet earth, but it is not wrestling on its laurels. The Google-owned platform this week announced a barrage of AI-powered features and tools, for both viewers and creators, that it is betting can help people make more content faster, and help viewers more specifically find what they are looking for. The company announced the tools at its annual Made on YouTube event in New York City, with CEO Neal Mohan taking the stage in Google’s office in a former shipping pier on the Hudson River. “Since the start of the year, we’ve launched over 3,000 product updates and improvements, keeping up with evolving viewer tastes and increasing creator ambitions,” Mohan said. “This is what it looks like to innovate in the YouTube era, an era where entertainment is built from the ground up by creators and the communities that fuel them.” For YouTube viewers, the biggest change will be the introduction of Custom Feeds, which will let users type what they are interested in in (think “help me find new DIY creators” or “witty podcasts for my 30 minute commute”), with the platform creating new tabs that will refresh with options in those defined areas. The platform is also adding new functionality to Ask YouTube, enabling followup questions and more specific search capabilities. On the creator front, some of the announcements drew applause and buzz from many of the creators in attendance. YouTube Studio can now suggest pacing and structure for videos, and help creators automatically A/B test thumbnails. Soon it will allow for A/B testing of videos, enabling different versions of content for different audiences. It is also rolling out a conversational editing assistant, letting users lean on YouTube’s apps to help it edit content using natural language prompts. Opt-in AI-powered comment moderation is also in the works, as is a voice detection tool that will join its current likeness detection program. “Our approach has always been to use AI to empower human creativity, and to do it responsibly,” Mohan told the crowd. Matt Shreder of Concourse Media is handling international sales. As Julia becomes increasingly consumed with discovering who is behind the deliveries, she turns to delivery driver Charlie (David Dastmalchian), her sister Tatiana (Anna Baryshnikov), and Whitney (Rhea Seehorn), a woman from her recovery group, for help. Her search eventually leads her to Lisa Barr (Jamie Lee Curtis), who has been receiving disturbingly familiar packages of her own.” The film marks the debut feature from writer-director Goldman. Executive producers include Russell Goldman, Britt Lower, Akshay Shah, Thomas Grabinski, Paris Jones, and Andre Ray. “The dream of any filmmaker is finding a distributor that understands your film and wants to put it in front of as many eyeballs as possible,” said Goldman. “ Sender isn’t the kind of film that fits neatly into a box, which makes it especially meaningful that the entire MPI and Dark Sky team has a real vision for its nationwide theatrical release. title: Andra Day To Play Wrongly Convicted Army Veteran In ‘Don’t Go Gentle’ From Deborah Riley Draper
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Andra Day To Play Wrongly Convicted Army Veteran In ‘Don’t Go Gentle’ From Deborah Riley Draper MIP London Comes To An End After Two Years; Organizers Launching New Event Alongside London Book Fair Liz Murdoch & Jane Featherstone’s Sister Group Takes Stake In Common Interest View All September 24, 2026 6:32am L-R: Andra Day, Len Cariou, Lonnie Chavis, Teyonah Parris, Alexandra Daddario, Finn Wittrock To Star In ‘Don’t Go Gentle’ From Deborah Riley Draper Emilynn Rose, Andrew Walker, Getty, Najah Chavis, Jacob Webster, Storm Santos, PMC EXCLUSIVE: Andra Day will star as a U.S. Army veteran trying to clear her name after being convicted of a crime she did not commit in Don’t Go Gentle . Len Cariou will play a retired judge who becomes involved with her case in the film, which Deborah Riley Draper writes and directs. Lonnie Chavis, Alexandra Daddario, Finn Wittrock and Teyonah Parris also star in the movie, which Draper has reworked from Stephen Belber’s play of the same name. Gerard Butler is a producer under his G-BASE banner, alongside Alan Siegel and Dan Kaslow. Crystine Zhang produces for Oval-5. Related Stories Festivals 'Is This Thing On?' Review: Bradley Cooper's Comedic Dissection Of A Marriage On The Rocks Is Indeed Right On - New York Film Festival Casting 'Percy Jackson': Andra Day Cast As Athena In Season 2 Of Disney+ Series Set in modern-day Buffalo, Don’t Go Gentle follows Tanya Jenkins, a mother and Army medic who was honorably discharged. She refuses to let a wrongful conviction become the final word on her life and ends up being pulled into the privileged but strained world of a former judge and his family. Watch on Deadline Cariou ( Blue Bloods ) is the retired judge, Lawrence Driver, whose history and sense of authority are challenged by Tanya’s presence. Chavis ( This Is Us ) plays Rasheed, Tanya’s teenage son, and Parris ( WandaVision ) is Ellen, Tanya’s half-sister. Daddario ( The White Lotus ) is Amelia, Lawrence’s architect daughter. Wittrock ( American Horror Story ) plays Ben, his troubled son. This marks Draper’s move into writing and directing narrative features. She is known for making award-winning docs including A&E’s James Brown: Say It Loud and OWN/Discovery+’s The Legacy of Black Wall Street . Speaking to Deadline from the Toronto set of the movie, Draper said: “ Don’t Go Gentle is completely reimagined from the play, but this is still a story about place, belonging and identity. In her quest to vindicate herself after being wrongly convicted, Tanya crosses paths with a retired judge who’s dying and ultimately her family moves in with him. There is a dynamic of these families understanding who they are, their place in America, understanding what home is, what legacy is and what entitlement is.” Day earned an Academy Award nom and won a Golden Globe for Best Actress for her portrayal of Billie Holiday in Lee Daniels’ The United States vs. Billie Holiday . “ Don’t Go Gentle challenges the idea that strength means suffering in silence,” she said. “What we accepted yesterday does not have to be what we accept today and Tanya exemplifies that. She is resilient and a healer. For her, every new environment and every obstacle is an opportunity to grow and improve conditions for herself, her son and her community.” Draper added that stories about what happens to women after military service are thin on the ground. “Women veterans in America are one of the most overlooked groups because the military system wasn’t necessarily set up for them,” she said. “They come home and often they are poorly served. Andra has embodied this character in so many ways. She’s done so much research about female veterans and African American female veterans.” Draper’s Atlanta-based label Coffee Bluff Pictures produces alongside G-BASE and Oval-5. title: Marlene Emilie Lyngstad Addresses First Reactions to Controversial Love Story ‘Cute’: ‘Maybe People Are Confronted by Their Own Monsters?’
full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:25am PT Marlene Emilie Lyngstad Addresses First Reactions to Controversial Love Story ‘Cute’: ‘Maybe People Are Confronted by Their Own Monsters?’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Marlene Emilie Lyngstad Addresses First Reactions to Controversial Love Story ‘Cute’: ‘Maybe People Are Confronted by Their Own Monsters?’ 31 minutes ago In ‘Tenzing,’ Jennifer Peedom Ensures the Iconic Himalayan Mountaineer Is Finally ‘the Protagonist of His Own Life’ 2 hours ago In Docuseries ‘Keinaan, Go Back to Somalia,’ Finnish-Somali YouTube Star Turns Racist Comments Into a Personal Statement 3 hours ago See All Samai Collado, San Sebastian Film Festival Marlene Emilie Lyngstad has ruffled some feathers at San Sebastián with her feature debut “ Cute .” “I find it interesting and exciting that the film creates such strong reactions,” she tells Variety . “It’s never explicit, so the discomfort must arise from the inner battles of the characters. Maybe people are confronted by their own monsters?” Related Stories Amazon's AWS Now Lets Streamers Deliver up to 10 Live Feeds on One Screen Nicholas Sparks’ ‘Counting Miracles’ Adaptation at Amazon to Be Helmed by ‘The Peanut Butter Falcon’ Filmmaker Tyler Nilson (EXCLUSIVE) Her lead, Richard, is certainly used to dealing with his own inner demons. Attracted to his girlfriend’s seven-year-old daughter, he leaves and hides in his old childhood home. There, he meets his mother’s caregiver, Stella, who likes to behave like a little girl. Also in front of the camera. Popular on Variety “I think there’s an important distinction between the guilt of someone who has abused a child and the guilt of someone with an unwanted attraction who’s determined not to act on it. My film deals with the latter,” emphasizes Lyngstad. “Richard is fighting an inner battle that confronts us with difficult but important questions: How can this person forge a decent life while carrying shame that can never be eliminated? Is this person also worthy of love?” “Cute” is a love story, she says. “It asks what love is. It’s about two adults, each broken in their own way, who long to be loved unconditionally.” While the media tends to feed people black-and-white narratives, people watch cinema “because they want more than that.” “I’m not interested in discomfort for its own sake, but I do think that some degree of unsettlement is inevitable when asking questions that might not have answers. I find humans uncomfortably contradictory, and I love it when cinema exposes these contradictions.” TrustNordisk handles sales for “Cute,” produced by Nordisk Film Production A/S (Denmark). It’s co-produced by Nordisk Film Production Ab, Film I Väst (Sweden) and Amarcord (Norway). Jan Gunnar Røise, who worked on her graduation film “Norwegian Offspring,” Karin Bertling, Kitt Maiken Mortensen and Molly Kirk Rasmussen star in the film. As well as newcomer Gina Jaqueline, who plays Stella. “I first met Gina while doing research for this film. She was a collector of the ‘cute’ aesthetic, and I was interested in understanding its appeal on grown-ups. When I told her about Stella, she opened up about her experience with OnlyFans and the online erotic market,” recalls Lyngstad. She asked Jaqueline to join as a consultant when developing the script. “She knew this universe firsthand. When we started the casting process, I decided to invite Gina, even though she had no formal acting training. She turned out to be a raw talent. She had the ability to lift the scenes from the page and deliver performances beyond my imagination.” “She was navigating the line between being exceptionally charming, vital, very vulnerable and haunted. I was very touched by her presence.” Lyngstad found the contrast between Røise and Jaqueline “especially exciting”: “It was Jan Gunnar’s precision and control against Gina’s playfulness and intuition,” she says. As proven by their first responses following the world premiere, cinema audiences have a complicated relationship with sexual imagery these days, even though anything is available online. “It’s hypocritical,” says the director. “That’s why I wanted to deal with the imagery provided by the internet. Images connecting childhood and sexuality are a part of pop culture and even mainstream pornography. A new territory of moral ambiguity has emerged. How should we navigate these blurred lines between fantasy, representation and exploitation?” She adds: “I think we don’t want to look at this. title: Israel-Gaza War Documentary ‘NAZA’ Sets Global Theatrical Release Plans
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 24, 2026 6:20am 'NAZA' Naza/The Guardian NAZA , the Israel – Gaza war documentary, has set plans for a global theatrical release from Sept. 28 after picking up the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival. The film from No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor will have a North American premiere at the New York Film Festival on Saturday, to be followed by a theatrical release starting Oct. 9 in the U.S. and now a global rollout. “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon,” Abraham and Szor said in a statement. Related Stories TV 'Made in Korea' Finale: Hyun Bin Reflects on the Message Behind Disney+'s Hit K-Drama Thriller Movies Rolf de Heer Named Jury President for Tokyo Film Festival For the film’s international release coming hot on the heels of the Venice premiere, The Guardian and partner mk2 Films have inked deals with theatrical distributors in 56 territories. Those markets include The Middle East, France, Canada, UK, Italy, Spain, Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Brazil and Central America. After the theatrical run globally, NAZA, executive produced by Jonathan Glazer ( The Zone of Interest ) and featuring testimony from 24 Israeli military officers outlining the systems and protocols they allege Israel uses to target and kill Palestinian civilians in Gaza, will stream on The Guardian website, for free. The film’s title, NAZA , comes from an acronym the Israeli military uses as a shorthand for civilian casualties. The film’s producers said the documentary has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel, and The Guardian was looking for ways to allow the film to be seen in Gaza and the West Bank. NAZA is produced by The Guardian and JW Films. Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and a NAZA producer, in his own statement said: “ NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years, but it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world. The initial response from those who’ve seen it shows audiences are engaging deeply with the urgent questions the film raises. We’re working with MK2 and international partners to bring the film to global audiences as soon as possible.” THR

full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:05am PT Brazil’s Desvia Filmes Enters New Era With Doubled Focus on Indie and Rachel Daisy Ellis’ San Sebastián Co-Pro Forum’s Buzzy ‘The Last Cruise’ Veteran British producer Ellis is ushering Desvia into its next chapter following Gabriel Mascaro's exit to launch Trema label alongside Paula Cosenza earlier this year By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Brazil’s Desvia Filmes Enters New Era With Doubled Focus on Indie and Rachel Daisy Ellis’ San Sebastián Co-Pro Forum’s Buzzy ‘The Last Cruise’ 1 hour ago Mauro Mueller’s ‘111 – Echoes From Halifax’ Might Chronicle Tragic 1998 Swissair Plane Crash, but This Is Not Your Regular Disaster Movie 2 hours ago San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference: 10 Takeaways From AI to ‘Obsession,’ YouTube and Why International Movies Could Dominate the Oscars 6 hours ago See All Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building Courtesy of Desvia Filmes Very few production companies can boast about landing major international festival premieres for every project in their slate. Brazil ’s Desvia Filmes is one of them, with all of its 16 features launching at festivals such as Berlin, Cannes, and Locarno. Founded in 2010 by “The Blue Trail” director Gabriel Mascaro and British producer Rachel Daisy Ellis – who has long been based in Recife – Desvia is behind films such as Bruno Santamaría’s “Six Months In the Pink and Blue Building,” Benjamin Naishtat’s “Rojo,” Manuel Abramovich’s “Pornomelancholia” and all of Mascaro’s films, including “Divine Love” and “Neon Bull.” Related Stories Mahershala Ali Finally Made His ‘Blade’ Film With ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Amazon's Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors' Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series 'Maxton Hall' Earlier this year, the company underwent a major transition, as Mascaro left Desvia to launch Trema alongside veteran producer Paula Cosenza. Trema will focus on international co-productions, scripted series and auteur-driven cinema with global reach, while Desvia will keep its laser-sharp focus on films, backing auteurs and filmmakers playing with form and genre. Popular on Variety Speaking with Variety out of San Sebastián , where she presented “The Last Cruise” at the festival’s prestigious Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum, Ellis reiterates how thrilled she is for Mascaro and Cosenza’s new venture and the opportunities it will open up for both companies. “It’s one big portfolio of projects now split between two production companies, and amplified in this sense,” she says. “For many years, Desvia worked almost exclusively on Gabriel’s projects, especially because the two of us had a very strong creative partnership. We’ve reached incredible heights together, but had arrived at a moment when both of us wanted to branch out, so it was an organic process.” The producer says she and Mascaro have “an incredible history together,” with “nothing stopping them” from working together again in the future. “For now, this setup makes it possible for him to work with new filmmakers, and for us at Desvia to bring new creative voices in.” And, while Desvia is indeed bringing in new voices into its slate, it is also currently at full steam ahead with Ellis’s own directorial projects, which include the documentary short “The Book of Colors,” feature docs “Drone” and “The Dream Conference,” and “The Last Cruise.” The latter sees the director step into fiction, mixing doc elements with a fictionalized narrative to tell the story of an elderly couple who decides to forego a retirement home in favor of spending their last years on a cruise. “It’s a project we’ve been researching for over two years, but I had the seed for the idea over 15 years ago,” she says. “I was in touch with someone from the British Council in Recife, who told me a crazy statistic: one of his main jobs was repatriation, and a lot of elderly Brits died on cruise ships, with their bodies being stored under the deck. He also told me a lot of retirees prefer to take one last big trip in life rather than settle into a care home, and many didn’t want to—or couldn’t—fly. So the option was a major around-the-world cruise.” The producer wanted to make a documentary about the phenomenon at first and then, during the pandemic, she read an article about the growing phenomenon of people choosing to live in these lavish boats as it costs less than living in many major cities during a cost of living crisis. “Once I read that article, the original idea came back into my mind, and I was set on making it happen.” “The Blue Trail” Courtesy of Guillermo Garza/Desvia Ellis has locked financing for production in Brazil, which was an important step given it is “not a cheap project.” The film requires her to follow a couple on a cruise for a year, with the subjects also filming themselves and their routine in this very particular environment. “This first-person point of view is very much part of the way I work as a director,” she says of the creative choice. “It’s a way of having access to a layer of intimacy I otherwise wouldn’t be able to capture. I also realized this film is about love and companionship. ‘Eros,’ my previous film, was also about this, and I feel this film is a continuation of my interest in how people communicate with their partners when they live on the periphery of the norm.” With Mascaro gone, long-term producing collaborator of Desvia, Camille Reis, became a partner and is now leading on several projects. Given Reis’s limited bandwidth, Ellis brought in renowned Argentinian producer Gema Juárez Allen (“Reas,” “Plaza Catedral”) to lead on “The Last Cruise,” with the duo seeking a co-production with Argentina. “I worked with Gema before; we worked on ‘Pornomelancholia’ together, and when I invited her to produce the project, she loved the idea,” says Ellis. “It’s been incredible working with her, and this partnership as a producer is beautiful to me, because I know what it feels like to have an incredible producer by your side and how that changes the project. Once she boarded ‘The Last Cruise,’ I knew we would be good to go.” As for the next steps with the company, the producer says they are “very focused on cinema.” “We haven’t had the drive to branch into TV or other formats. When I look back at all the projects I’ve worked on with Gabriel, and all the co-productions we’ve worked on, they are all very daring films, with a latent desire to provoke. This is something that attracts me both as a producer and director, and we want to continue to bring Desvia towards that pathway.” And it is indeed an exciting pathway, with Desvia’s slate including Clarisa Navas’s “They Burn the Same Way,” which was a buzzy project at this year’s Venice Gap-Financing Bridge; Filipa Reis’ “Lontra,” a co-production with Portugal, Spain, France and Argentina; and “Who Named the Earth?” an exciting feature debut by Indigenous filmmaker Wara. ‘Kill Jackie,’ Starring a Glamorous, Lethal Catherine Zeta-Jones, Acquired by Warner Bros. title: ‘Real Housewives of Rhode Island’ Star Alicia Carmody on How the Bravo Series Changed Her Life: “I Never Knew I Could Work This Hard”
full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 24, 2026 6:00am Alicia Carmody of 'The Real Housewives of Rhode Island.' Noam Galai/Bravo Alicia Carmody’s life has done a full 180 since it was announced she joined The Real Housewives of Rhode Island cast not even a year ago. Five months after the show debuted on Bravo , the Housewife is deep into filming on the highly anticipated second season, but she squeezed in some time to chat with The Hollywood Reporter about her new partnership with Ferrero celebrating Adultoween. “I love Halloween . I love snacks. I love Ferrero. I love a Butterfinger. I love a Kinder Egg. So it kind of just like all worked out,” Alicia says when asked why she wanted to partner with the food company behind snacks such as Nutella, Kinder and Tic Tac. Related Stories TV Kim Kardashian Debuts New Reality Show 'Team Moms: Baseball': Where to Watch Online TV Khloé Kardashian on 'The Girls' Future, 'The Kardashians' Longevity and Her Sephora Fragrances Alicia adds of the partnership, “Halloween has always been one of my favorite times of year. It’s really about embracing that sense of play and not taking yourself too seriously. That’s exactly what Adultoween is about: Giving adults permission to be creative and have fun again, the way we did as kids. And honestly, snacking is such a huge part of that nostalgia for me — Ferrero has always been part of my Halloween memories, so partnering with them for this felt really natural.” Ferrero’s Halloween collection includes Kinder Joy x Stranger Things Eggs, Kinder Bueno Halloween Lay Down Bags, Butterfinger Skulls, Keebler Spookie Fudge Stripes, Mother’s Eerie Critters and Kinder Joy Glow in the Dark Halloween Eggs. When asked if partnering with brands is something she was looking forward to after becoming a Housewife, Alicia admits, “I actually really never thought I was going to even be a Housewife. I really didn’t know what to expect, to be honest.” Alicia Carmody for Ferrero. Courtesy Bravo revealed in May that Rhode Island was pacing as the network’s second-biggest series across platforms, behind only The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills , the longtime ratings winner of the franchise. Alicia says that the cast “had no clue” their show would be so well received, and she believes viewers resonated with her story because she “was so honest about my life.” Among the topics she discussed on season one were her 10-year engagement to Billy Kitsilis and her desire to be more involved in their business, Pizza Mamma. “I don’t know how to not be myself, and I think people could see that, you know,” she says when asked why fans resonated with her. “I shared my family, my aunts, building a business with my fiancé. I just think that I was so honest about my life.” Being a Housewife is a full-time job, and Alicia says it’s been hard work. “It’s a full-time job, but I didn’t know that. I was like, I’m gonna film going out to dinner with my girlfriends, having a cocktail, a drama here and there, you know,” she says. “I never knew I could work this hard, and it keeps you young. It keeps you moving. You’re always pushing yourself to different limits.” Alicia is partaking in Bravo Fan Fest Charleston this October, just ahead of Halloween. It will be her first fan event as a Housewife, and she’s preparing to “take up every moment that I can.” As for details about season two of The Real Housewives of Rhode Island , she remains tight-lipped, but hints at a potential story to come. “It’s a lot of work, to wedding plan,” she says. Would she ever let Bravo film her wedding? “You never know. I don’t even know what day it is right now, so you never know what [it will be] like when it actually happens. I mean, it’s been 10 years that we’ve been engaged.” With the launch of her partnership with Ferrero, Alicia gave her Instagram followers a peek into how she celebrates Halloween, while announcing a giveaway that will see a winner receive Ferrero Halloween goodies. Of what she loves most about the holiday, the Housewife said, “I love that Halloween, you can be creative and you can be whatever. You can make yourself into whatever you want.” “Adultoween started as an insight the Ferrero Group discovered and has grown into a cultural movement,” said Chad Stubbs, chief marketing officer of Ferrero North America. “We’re excited to see where this year’s trends land and how they’ll shape the way we engage and show up for our fans in bigger and better ways this Halloween and beyond.” THR

title: How Bob Chapek’s Disney Dream Turned Into an Instant Nightmare: Bob Iger “Wanted to See Me Fail”
full_text: × Skip to main content Former CEO Bob Chapek, right, with his predecessor and successor, Bob Iger. Courtesy Disneyland Resort/Christian Thompson Of all the stories and tales that Disney tells so well, perhaps none proved as fanciful, and lasted as long, as the fantasy that Bob Iger was going to retire. Sure, he thought about it. And he talked about it. Bob’s public contemplations of retirement became a Hollywood tradition, like the Oscars, only it occurred slightly less frequently. Still, it was something of its own production. On different occasions, including that first conversation in my office when he asked me who I thought should replace him (and I said “me”), Bob Iger dropped more breadcrumbs than Hansel and Gretel, but they never actually led anywhere. First he was going to enter politics, then, after some initial feelers, thought better of it. Then, two years later, he publicly flirted with bringing an NFL franchise to Los Angeles, which never gained momentum. Each time, the entire management class underneath him readied for what could be a moment of transition. A number of us felt like the slipper would fit on our feet, if only Bob Iger would take it off in the first place. Still, I did feel like I was being prepared for advancement. After that initial conversation about who his replacement should be, I started being invited to more functions, like board dinners, with corporate leadership. Those early engagements with the board also allowed me to participate in discussions about the company’s future. Bob’s long-standing relationship with many board members created powerful alliances for him, and he often used them to his advantage. As long as we were on the same team, those strong alliances were providing effective support for me as well. By the end of 2016, my two main competitors for the top spot, Jay Rasulo and Tom Staggs, were gone. I realized I was genuinely in the running for the role. Brooks Barnes of The New York Times had called Tom “the only obvious candidate for the job When Tom left, the chatter shifted, with some placing their bets on either Kevin Mayer or me crossing the finish line first. Kevin had also held key executive positions, including overseeing Disney’s acquisitions of Pixar, Marvel, and Lucasfilm, among others. The question of who Bob’s successor would be took another unexpected turn in 2017, and by then, a lot had changed for me. I now had an office in Burbank as chairman of parks and resorts. The successful completion of Shanghai Disney had elevated my standing with Bob, and talk of his retirement was heating up again. When he asked to meet with me shortly before Thanksgiving, I couldn’t help but wonder if this was the moment I had been waiting for. After a few years of waiting, working, and delivering profound value from my position in parks, I let myself fall into the trap once again. By the fall of 2017, Bob had indicated that he was preparing to retire, and this time, he seemed serious about it. Just before the Thanksgiving holiday, he visited the headquarters of Imagineering,, the creative design division that was one of my responsibilities as chairman of Disney Parks, Experiences, and Products. Around five o’clock, at the end of a fun but exhausting day, he asked if he could see me before he left the building. He followed me into my Imagineering office and shut the door. “Bob, I have some news,” he said, his gaze unwavering. My heart began to race. Could this be it? “Bob, we are buying Fox, and I’m staying three more years. Have a great holiday,” he said bluntly before getting up and walking out. It had happened again. I felt as if I were on a football team lining up on the fifty-yard line for a drive and making it all the way to the five-yard line, only to be pushed back by holding calls, sacks, or too many players on the field. In football terms, at the very least, I was dealing with false starts and delay-of-game penalties that seemed completely arbitrary. That holiday season, I felt dejected, thinking that I might never get my chance to truly achieve my dream. Still, I had a job to do. So I did what I always do: I kept my head down and worked harder. Parks was doing well, and the best way to get the role I wanted was to be great at it. Kevin, from the reports of many, was not so subtle in his efforts to ramp up his public relations campaign for his candidacy—and in some circles he was anointed as the favorite to be Bob’s successor. Nevertheless, Bob and other insiders repeatedly assured me that, despite Kevin’s maneuvers for the coveted position, they did not consider him a serious candidate. I had to push aside any thoughts of finishing as the runner-up, because I would consider that a great disappointment—or, as I had told my wife, Cindy, a failure. To be clear, pushing aside thoughts and frustrations is easier when you have one of the best jobs at one of the biggest companies in the world. There’s always plenty to do, and when you’re a competitor, you’re always looking for ways to improve your score, which, for me, meant Disney’s bottom line. Shanghai and Disneyland Paris were growing, and our new pricing systems in parks and cruises were paying dividends, literally. Our earnings report in November 2019 touted that revenues for the quarter increased 8 percent to $6.7 billion, and park operating income increased 17 percent to $1.4 billion. The next month, I was working in my office, getting ready to spend the holidays with my family, when Bob requested another meeting with me. I couldn’t help but think of the meeting years before when he had come in, also right before a holiday, to tell me he was staying. He did have news. In December 2019, he came into my office, closed the door, and this time delivered some different news. “Bob, I want you to know. I’m leaving.” I didn’t roll my eyes. At least, I didn’t mean to. In my mind, let’s just say I was less than convinced. Okay, Bob , I thought. Then he said the words that would change my life forever. “I’ve told the board you’re my replacement.” I barely said anything. It wasn’t until Susan Arnold, the board’s lead independent director, called me the next day that I started to think this long-imagined fantasy might be real. So, there I was one day in January 2020, sitting in The Rotunda, the company’s executive dining room located in Burbank atop Team Disney—the Michael D. Eisner Building. Susan Arnold had asked if I wanted to get lunch. While The Rotunda is a place reserved for executives whose titles grant them the privilege of entry, the seating arrangement is more reminiscent of a high school lunchroom, except that everyone is much wealthier and more powerful. Each table represents a level in the company’s hierarchy, and the seating is determined by each employee’s rank. If Bob Iger were in town, he would sit at his preferred seat at essentially the twelve o’clock of the circular arrangement of tables. If not, the next-highest-ranking person would take his place. It was the third week of January when Susan and I finally took our seats at this head table in the dining room. Unsure of what to expect, I wanted to be ready for anything. I had eaten at the head table many times before, but this was still an event for me. I was here with the head of our board. People saw. We ordered salads and made small talk. But in truth, I didn’t have much of an appetite. Before we started eating, Susan looked at me and said directly, “So I understand Bob has spoken with you.” I simply nodded in response. “Well, it’s going to happen, and it’s going to happen fast. Bob has decided relatively abruptly that he’s done, and the job is yours.” Suddenly, the clinking of silverware and murmurs of nearby conversations faded away as I tried to process what I had just heard. I couldn’t believe it; I had so many questions. However, I was extremely careful to avoid asking the wrong ones, which could lead to another setback. I had been toyed with for six years. It seemed like I was on the goal line. The last thing I wanted to do was draw a flag. “How fast are we talking?” I asked her. I suddenly started thinking about the logistics—not just of doing the job, but of the announcement, which I assumed would be a thoughtful, drawn-out process. I was envisioning engaging with board members and some press, followed by a publicity tour and some meet and greets with key stakeholders over the next few months. “It’s coming within two weeks, not months,” she said, her voice steady and firm. As soon as the lunch was over, I called Cindy. At the time, we’d been married for nearly forty years, and if anyone knew how much this meant to me, it was her. After more than a decade of waiting, I was, in fact, getting “it.” Finally. It was a victory for me, but it would come at a cost to others. Kevin Mayer, the presumed front-runner to some, announced he was leaving shortly after my appointment was made official. Kevin’s departure made him the third of Bob Iger’s top lieutenants over the last decade, along with Tom Staggs and Jay Rasulo, to leave. Each of them believed he was the front-runner to be anointed team captain, convinced the job was his. Instead, in the end, Bob had just been toying with them. During my follow-up conversations with Bob, he expressed a desire to remain involved and help me succeed in his former position. He also voiced his frustrations, saying, “I’m ready to leave, Bob. I’m sick of the earnings calls and all the board meetings.” Those familiar with the situation suspected there were other reasons behind his decision to leave. One possibility was that his compensation wasn’t meeting his expectations, despite his receiving more than $100 million in stock awards from the Fox deal. Although he was a top player in the industry, his pay was considerably less than that of executives at Universal, Paramount, and Fox, all of which have more concentrated shareholder control from a smaller number of influential large investors versus widespread retail investors like Disney. Later, I would discover there might be other reasons behind his “abrupt” decision. After all the years of uncertainty and playmaking, I was surprised by how quickly everything came to a head. The timeline of my appointment moved at such a breakneck pace that I didn’t have the opportunity to meet with a single board member on the matter of my ascension and the transition. As these events unfolded in a whirlwind, I learned that while Bob Iger would no longer be CEO, the board had agreed to allow him to stay on as “executive chairman of the board” and “creative director” for an additional two years. This meant I would have to report to both the board and Bob, although the interpretation of that varied depending on whom you asked. It certainly was confusing to me, as the story kept changing. Initially, I wasn’t too concerned about this arrangement. After all, Bob had always supported me. Why wouldn’t he continue to do so? My naiveté about my dream job was about to end rather abruptly. When Bob Iger released a statement naming me as his successor, the news stunned most people at the company, catching them entirely off guard. By the end of my first day on the job, I realized that I, too, had been caught off guard—and not in a good way. As part of the announcement and rollout, we had arranged an interview with CNBC, with interviews with other outlets to follow. Sitting in matching directors’ chairs on the Disney studio lot, Bob and I were only a few minutes into our first interview with CNBC when I noticed things weren’t going as expected. Bob usually appeared confident and optimistic in interviews, but he clearly didn’t feel that way during this one. I quickly understood I needed to do everything possible to avoid making the situation a fiasco. I could almost feel the daggers Bob was hurling my way. When he introduced me to the world as his successor, he initially had said we had worked “extremely well” together. Seconds later, he went out of his way to clarify that “Actually, our senior management team has worked together quite well.” That was it. In response, throughout the exchange, I made every effort to compliment him for all the magic he had created for the company and acknowledge what an outstanding mentor he had been to me. “I plan to follow in his footsteps and recognize I have some big shoes to fill,” I said. “We have a solid strategy, and I intend to continue implementing every part of that strategy.” Whenever I glanced in Bob’s direction, his expression was ice-cold, and his shifting body language spoke volumes about how miserable and uncomfortable he felt. There were moments when he even appeared angry, with his jaws clenched. Bob Iger was botching the handoff because I believe he didn’t want to let go of the ball. What I didn’t know then is that the reality of that truth would leave no room for recovery. It was so obvious that a reporter who had been covering the CEO transition shared his observation with me following the CNBC interview: it was apparent to him that Bob regretted everything and that the spotlight on me frustrated him. Why? Because I was now the one providing the play-by-play while he was relegated to adding color commentary. I didn’t respond to the reporter. He was right. The day after my announcement, I flew to New York to meet with investors and participate in more media interviews. I still hadn’t even been inside my new office at Disney, which I learned would not be the same one Bob had occupied as CEO. Famous for liking to get to the office early and working out, Bob had a private shower in his office. “You don’t need a shower in your office,” he told me. I didn’t want to make things any more awkward than they already were, so I readily acquiesced. I didn’t care about the trappings of a fancy office. I was just excited to have the job. I took a different office. The symbolism loomed large, as I would later experience. While I might have landed the position, it seemed like Bob was now doing to me what he had previously done to Kevin, Tom, and Jay: playing me. Two weeks later, the concerns I had during our CNBC interview began to play out openly. We were scheduled to hold our annual shareholder meeting in Raleigh in March, just before everything shut down because of COVID. On the plane, I had asked Bob how he wanted to handle the Q&A from the board. He was aware I had never run a television network before, let alone a number of them, between ABC, ESPN, and other cable channels. Given my quick appointment, he understood there were still aspects of the company’s operations that were unfamiliar to me. “How do you want to divide up these questions, Bob?” I asked, feeling increasingly anxious as my palms began to sweat. This was my first time addressing the shareholders as the new CEO. “Oh, no. I’m not getting up there,” he informed me. “It’s all you.” “I’ve had the job just two weeks, Bob,” I reminded him. “Well, you have a binder. Study it,” he responded dismissively. At that moment, I was 100 percent convinced he wanted to see me fail. Of course, the very first question was about TV. It came from a conservative activist who threw me a curveball. He wanted to know how I could sleep at night knowing the liberal bent of ABC News. He proceeded to provide example after example before basically ending with, essentially, “What do you think of that, new guy?” ABC News was a wholly owned subsidiary of Disney. So, as CEO, I was responsible for its operations and, apparently, alleged political bent. I responded that ABC held itself to the highest standards of objectivity and balanced coverage. I felt my answer hit his curveball satisfactorily. However, the feedback I received from both sides of the political spectrum within the company indicated neither side was totally satisfied. The liberal wing said I should have told him he was full of it, and those on the right thought I should have been more sympathetic. It seemed there was no way to win. In that moment, though, Bob Iger had let me down. Unfortunately, that wasn’t the last curveball that day. While flying back from the Raleigh meeting, our finance chief, Christine McCarthy, suggested, “Hey, why not have our first one-on-one meeting now?” Although it seemed like a normal request, Bob reacted explosively. “How could you dare disrespect me by having your first one-on-one in front of me?” he shouted, his face flushed and visibly upset. In all the years we had worked together, this was the first time I had seen him demonstrate anger. We rode most of the rest of the way in relative silence. As we flew above a country that was only beginning to confront a global pandemic, I, too, was realizing just how difficult my life was about to become. title: Terence Winter Teams With  ‘Age of Disclosure’ Director to Adapt UFO Insider’s Story
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 6:00am Terence Winter Brigitte Lacombe Emmy-winning writer Terence Winter is teaming up with the filmmaker behind the indie documentary hit The Age of Disclosure to adapt an upcoming memoir that purports to reveal the behind-the-scenes story of the U.S. government’s cover-up of UFOs. The Sopranos and The Wolf of Wall Street writer will tackle the forthcoming book Out of the Shadows by former senior U.S. intelligence official Jay Stratton, who is considered the senior-most former government official to come forward claiming the existence of non-human intelligent life. Related Stories TV Vincent Pastore, the Mobster "Big Pussy" on 'The Sopranos,' Dies at 80 TV 'The Sopranos' Creator Says Hollywood Is "Going Back to Greed and Fear" in Trump Era The project, which is seeking distribution, is spearheaded by Age of Disclosure director-producer Dan Farah. “For all of human history, mankind has wondered whether we are the only intelligent life in the universe,” Winter said in a statement. “Jay Stratton’s shocking true story answers that question and more as it delves into the world of the U.S. government’s investigation of UAP and non-human intelligent life. It’s a riveting journey into a world the public knows little about. Jay is the key-man in the U.S. government’s modern-day investigation of UAP. While his decades of work have been in the shadows, it has changed the course of history and I couldn’t be more excited to bring his story to the screen.” “ Out of the Shadows has the propulsive storytelling of a high-stakes political thriller,” added Farah. “It brings you behind the scenes of the U.S. government’s investigation of the biggest mystery of all time. At the center of the story is the deeply personal, harrowing toll Jay’s pursuit of the truth had on him and his family.” Stratton cofounded the Advanced Aerospace Weapons System Application Program (AAWSAP), the first official U.S. government program to investigate UAP since the closure of the Air Force’s Project Blue Book in 1969. For 16 years, Stratton reportedly investigated UAP and non-human intelligent life on behalf of the federal government. In Age of Disclosure , Stratton declared, “I have seen, with my own eyes, non-human craft and non-human beings.” “It’s time for the world to learn the truth,” Stratton said in a statement. “There is far too much at stake. UAP activity over our nation’s sensitive military and nuclear sites is an ongoing issue.” Out of the Shadows will be published in the U.S. by HarperCollins imprint William Morrow on Oct. 13. The project marks the latest in a wave of UFO-related projects, which earlier this year included Steven Spielberg’s film Disclosure Day . Public interest in the topic has surged in the wake of a succession of media reports, lawmakers and whistleblowers making claims about unidentified anomalous phenomena. THR
