title: ‘The Swan’ Unmasked: Inside the Most Sadistic Reality Show Ever
full_text: ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection The mere mention of “ The Swan ” is enough to send chills down one’s spine. Created by former Telemundo exec Nely Galán, the Fox reality series selected 16 female contestants — from over 250,000 applicants — who were so-called “ugly ducklings” and subjected them to a 90-day ordeal of extreme plastic surgery, dentistry, training and crash dieting (with a little bit of therapy thrown in) to transform them into what its panel of “experts” deemed “attractive” before making them compete in “the ultimate beauty pageant,” where the women vied against one another for the ultimate prize of being crowned The Swan. Related Stories Emmys in Talks to Move to Amazon Prime Video Under New Licensing Arrangement, as the Broadcast Wheel Deal Ends (EXCLUSIVE) Amazon's AWS Now Lets Streamers Deliver up to 10 Live Feeds on One Screen In a review for Entertainment Weekly, Gillian Flynn, the future author of “Gone Girl,” called it “a foul blend of condescension and self-obsession” and “a misogynistic mix of TV’s twin vices: commercialism and conformity.” Popular on Variety The show’s first season debuted in April 2004 and was a smash hit, attracting 9 million viewers across America. But ratings plummeted in Season 2 amid heavy backlash to the show’s inherent ugliness, and it was canceled. “The Swan” has since ranked atop most lists for the “Worst Reality TV Series in History” and represents the cultural nadir of the image-obsessed early aughts. Now, the new documentary “The Swan: Behind the Mirror” examines the notorious reality series and the carnival of horrors its participants endured. Directed by Erin Lee Carr (“I Love You, Now Die: The Commonwealth V. Michelle Carter”) and premiering Sept. 29 on Hulu, the film tackles the show from all angles, including interviews with a dozen former contestants, show producers, trainers, cultural commentators and even one of its plastic surgeons, painting it as an enterprise that preyed on those with self-esteem issues in order to chase ratings. “They were not looking for people that had their life together,” says Carr. “They were looking for people who were, in my mind, vulnerable, and when you isolate people for 90 days who have already expressed that they have mental health issues, it’s going to go sideways.” Kristy Garza was interested in “The Swan” because she was exiting the military and ready for a life change. “I’d always struggled with self-esteem issues not because of my ability, but my appearance,” she tells Variety. “I’d always been a tomboy and wanted to feel like the prettiest girl in the room.” Also, after Kristy gave birth she “had cow teats at 23 years old.” She applied and was accepted for its first season. But things seemed off immediately following her surgeries. “My alarm bells started going off when we got to the apartments in Marina Del Rey and they showed us that all the reflective surfaces were covered,” she recalls. “I’d signed my life away in this contract and you’re already giving me surprises, so what else is going on?” Indeed, the 16 women on the show were trapped in apartments with no reflective surfaces — even CDs were confiscated by producers — and would have to request permission to leave via their Nextel walkie-talkies. They came to call it “Pretty Prison.” “There were times that I would call on the radio and no one would answer, so you get stir-crazy,” Kristy remembers. Kristy Garza in “The Swan: Behind the Mirror.” Disney There was no seeing family or friends, contestants were forced to work out six days a week (sometimes twice a day) while recovering from myriad plastic surgeries and had to adhere to a strict diet of 800-1,200 calories a day, courtesy of Jenny Craig. “There were so many of us that didn’t shit for a week,” Kristy shares in the doc. “The Swan” boasted of shelling out $250,000 on each contestant to cover their cosmetic surgeries, training, dieting and therapy, and producers drilled that sum into their heads throughout the entire process. “We were constantly being told, ‘You can leave, but if you do you’ll owe us for everything we’ve done!’” claims Kristy. If that weren’t enough, the beauty pageant element of the show wasn’t even revealed to contestants until after their surgeries were performed, while they were in recovery. Carl Buehl, a senior producer on the first season of “The Swan,” says this mandate came down from Fox executives to up the ante, posing the question, “Aren’t you tearing down everything we’ve done for them?” This curveball felt particularly manipulative to Kristy. “I came in because I have self-esteem issues and now you’re going to make me compare myself to everybody on a national stage while I’m still building myself up?” she exclaims. “I’m super pissed to this day. We were grossly mishandled and disrespected. You can’t invite somebody to play a game with you and then change the rules in the middle of the game. It was bullshit .” Season 2 was even more exploitive. For its big twist, sisters Kari and Gina Bravata were pitted against each other as contestants — only Gina’s participation was kept secret from Kari. The siblings were given the code names “Mark” and “Greg” so as not to spoil the surprise, and if Gina happened to spill the beans her contract stipulated that she was liable for $5 million plus attorney’s fees. “It was mean and it was cold and it was heartless. I’m still so bitter and so angry,” Kari attests. “I think they ultimately tried to break our bond, which is never going to happen because we’re stronger than them.” Kari and Gina Bravata in “The Swan: Behind the Mirrror.” Disney Far and away the most odious talking head in the documentary is Dr. Randal Haworth, one of the show’s two plastic surgeons. “There are no victims in life, only volunteers,” he declares. The women recall Haworth summoning them to a garage where they were pressured to undress and have fully nude photos taken of themselves as rock ‘n’ roll music blared. Though done under the guise of “before and after” plastic surgery photos, Haworth reveals in the film that the nudes were really for a coffee table book he was cooking up that never saw the light of day. Kari only learned about the coffee table book idea during the making of the doc. “It was a shock and it makes me feel sick,” she asserts. “We were told we had to do it and I remember crying in the middle of it.” And then she almost died. Since production has never been transparent about exactly what went down during her surgery, Kari has only her blurry memory combined with the accounts of cameramen who were in the operating room documenting it — until they were removed. “From what I’ve heard, they tried to wake me up and take me off anesthesia, pulled the tube out expecting me to wake up, and I didn’t,” Kari recounts. “During me not waking up, my lungs filled with fluid and my oxygen started dropping. It got to a low enough point that all the cameras got icked out, and that’s the extent of what I know happened.” She shakes her head: “I don’t think I’ll ever know what happened. I would love, for my own medical history, to know the extent of what happened, but I have absolutely no idea.” While “The Swan: Behind the Mirror” contains loads of access, two key players are noticeably absent: its creator Nely Galán and the show’s chief plastic surgeon, Dr. Terry Dubrow . Carr says she had “many conversations” with Galán about participating in the doc, but her demands — an executive producer credit and a degree of editorial control — proved too much. Since Galán owned the footage to “The Swan,” Carr and her team were forced to get creative, having subjects comment on scenes from the show being played on an iPad so they qualified as fair use. As for Dubrow, Carr says he “wanted a sum of money that would never make sense for a documentarian to pay an expert,” adding it was “under $100,000 for one interview.” “The Swan” Season 1 beauty pageant. ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection Dubrow, whose name may sound familiar from his role as the husband to “The Real Housewives of Orange County” star Heather Dubrow, opened up about his “The Swan” experience during a recent appearance on the podcast “We Need to Talk With Paul C. Brunson.” According to Dubrow, the show had been approved for a third season that was poised to be even more outrageous than Season 2. “We’re casting the third season, and because reality TV was really pushing the envelope at the time, we were going to do some crazy casting. We were going to have triplets. And because there were two surgeons, I was going to operate on two, [Haworth] was going to operate on one, and we were going to see how different they looked,” explained a chuckling Dubrow. However, when Peter Ligouri took over as entertainment chairman at Fox, one of his first orders of business was canceling “The Swan.” A number of ex-“Swan” contestants in the documentary contend that they experienced health complications following the show, from veneers falling out and gum disease — the show’s resident dentist, Dr. Sherri Worth, had her license revoked in 2017 for scamming clients — to more serious ones. Kristy discovered that she had two large aneurysms on her aorta and had to have a pair of open-heart surgeries. “It turns out I was born with a bicuspid aortic valve, which somebody on the show should have noticed when I was going through the health screening,” she says. Kari was confined to a wheelchair and had to have her gall bladder removed. “They told me it was probably from starving myself [on the show],” she says. Kristy and Kari say they and the other “Swan” contestants haven’t thought about filing a class-action lawsuit against the makers of the show, but the two found solace during the making of Carr’s documentary, which gave them much-needed closure. The final sequence of “The Swan: Behind the Mirror” sees the 12 women who participated in the film reunite for a celebratory dinner, reveling in each other’s company. “The documentary has been the most healing I’ve been able to do in the past 22 years,” offers Kristy. “Erin made me feel valued and seen. I didn’t even know how much I needed this. I thought I’d gotten past it after all these years, but I’d just compartmentalized it. We went from trauma and drama to this awesome sisterhood.” “It was healing in a way that you can’t even put into words,” adds Kari. “The weight that was lifted through this, and the girls that I can lean on, was healing and strengthened this bond that we have. I can’t wait for everyone to hear our story.” Loading comments... title: Terence Winter To Adapt Jay Stratton’s ‘Out Of The Shadows’ Memoir About Investigating Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena As TV Series
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Terence Winter To Adapt Jay Stratton’s ‘Out Of The Shadows’ Memoir About Investigating Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena As TV Series HBO’s Casey Bloys & Par’s George Cheeks Go To ‘War’ Together: Execs’ Joint Premiere Appearance Creates Intrigue With WBD Merger Closing ‘A Man On The Inside’ To End With Season 3; Netflix Comedy Starring Ted Danson Sets Returning Cast, Guest Stars & New Mystery As Production Starts View All September 24, 2026 6:00am Terence Winter ( Boardwalk Empire, Tulsa King ) is set to develop a TV series based on the upcoming memoir by former senior U.S. intelligence official Jay Stratton , the central figure in the U.S. Government’s modern investigation of unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) and non-human intelligent life. Winter has partnered on the project with Dan Farah , director/producer of the recent UAP documentary The Age of Disclosure, who had acquired the film and TV rights to the book. As the Chief of Air & Space Warfare in the Defense Warning Office of the Defense Intelligence Agency, Stratton specialized in emerging and disruptive aerospace technologies, ultimately focusing on investigating UAP. Related Stories Books Jay Stratton, Former Director Of U.S Government's Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, Unveils Title & Release Date For William Morrow Memoir Documentary Oscar-Contending Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Doc 'The Age Of Disclosure' Becomes VOD Phenomenon, Outperforming 'One Battle After Another' & More “In the early days of my investigation into UAP and non-human intelligent life, my work was so classified I couldn’t even tell my wife and kids that I had learned we are not alone in the universe or about any of the paradigm shift information I was learning,” Stratton said. “I had to live a double life, where the front door to my house served as a boundary between two distinct identities… but that all changed when we started having UAP activity and encounters with non-human intelligent life at our house and my wife and kids saw it with their own eyes.” Watch on Deadline Winter, who executive produces via his Cold Front Productions, noted that Stratton’s story has elements of some of his favorite shows and movies, Homeland, The Americans, The Hunt for Red October, All The President’s Men, Spotlight, and The Big Short. “For all of human history, mankind has wondered whether we are the only intelligent life in the universe,” Winter said. “Jay Stratton’s shocking true story answers that question and more as it delves into the world of the U.S. Government’s investigation of UAP and non-human intelligent life. It’s a riveting journey into a world the public knows little about.” Stratton’s memoir Out of the Shadows will be published in the U.S. by HarperCollins imprint William Morrow on Oct. 13. “ Out of the Shadows has the propulsive storytelling of a high-stakes political thriller,” Farah said. “It brings you behind the scenes of the U.S. Government’s investigation of the biggest mystery of all time. At the center of the story is the deeply personal, harrowing toll Jay’s pursuit of the truth had on him and his family. We intend to fully explore that in our show.” Winter, an Oscar nominee for The Wolf of Wall Street, won four Emmys for his work on The Sopranos . He created and executive produced HBO’s Boardwalk Empire and most recently served as executive producer/showrunner on Taylor Sheridan’s Paramount+ series Tulsa King. Winter is repped by CAA. title: Judge Orders White House to Restore Access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 24, 2026 5:42am Journalists gather in the Brady Press Briefing Room before going into the Oval Office at the White House on Sept. 18, 2026. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images A federal judge has ordered the White House to restore access to CNN , MS NOW and Politico, just days after President Trump had banned the outlets from the complex. Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, released his decision overnight Wednesday into Thursday, meaning that the reporters could return to the complex as early as today. “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action,” said Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr, attorney for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter . Trump said last week that he was banning the three outlets from the White House, and subsequently justified it by citing vague concerns around national security. The White House TV pool has since been suspended, with CNN not able to participate. In the Temporary Restraining Order, Kelly wrote that after examining the facts, the plaintiffs made a strong enough argument to warrant the decision. For example, the White House had renewed CNN reporter Betsy Klein’s pass months after some of the reporting it cited to justify her ban had been published. “Plaintiffs are also likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process. The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest.” he wrote in the ruling. “Defendants do not dispute that Plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to b heard before their hard passes were revoked.” He also poured cold water on the national security claims made by President Trump in recent days. “Nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns. Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly Wrote. “And even the justifications provided to Plaintiffs after this case was filed are ambiguous about the true purpose of the revocations: while Defendants’ letters to Plaintiffs mention national security concerns, they purport to identify reporting that “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods,” leaving open the possibility that all the stories fall into the later bucket, rather than the former.” THR

title: CAPA Deputy Director Unveils Sean Connery Doc; Talks Mission To Expand French Company’s International Reach
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie The Guardian To Offer ‘NAZA’ For Free On Website After Theatrical Run & Is Exploring Ways To Show Doc In Israel & Palestinian Territories ‘Maserati: The Brothers’ Actress Maya Talem Signs With MAD Celebrity ‘Ray Gunn’ Trailer: Netflix Adds Limited Theatrical Release For Brad Bird’s Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson-Voiced Animated Sci-Fi View All September 24, 2026 5:04am Sally Blake/Sean Connery with his wife artist Micheline Roquebrune at The Metropolitan Opera in 2006 Courtesy.Getty Images for The Metropolitan Opera EXCLUSIVE: A documentary promising unprecedented behind-the-scenes insight into the life of late Scottish star Sean Connery is in the works at Paris-based factual film and TV production company CAPA . Titled Sean Connery: The Untold Story , it is being developed and directed by French journalist and TV presenter Stéphanie Renouvin, who is the granddaughter of the James Bond star and his second wife, the French Moroccan painter Micheline Roquebrune. It follows Renouvin’s 2022 mini-series Mme Sean Connery , which focused on her grandmother and was made primarily for a French audience. Related Stories News French Film & TV Sectors Sound Alarm Over Cuts To State Broadcaster Budget; Say They Are At Odds With Macron's Lumière Summit Pledges Acquisitions Disney+ Seals EMEA Deal For Season 1 Of TF1 Hit 'Cat's Eyes' As Season 2 Gets October Launch Date Sean Connery: The Untold Story is one of the upcoming titles currently being developed by Sally Blake , the newly appointed Deputy Director of CAPA, which is part of the Studio TFI group. Watch on Deadline “We developed it here. It’s a coproduction with Canal Plus and Sky has come onboard in the UK,” says Blake, also citing London-based Embankment and Glasgow-based Boy 313 as coproducers. Blake, who was appointed to her new role in early September, will work closely with CAPA MD Patrice Lorton, with a mission to “internationalize” the company’s activities and specific goals to connect it with new territories and sources of funding. She says the upcoming Sean Connery documentary ticks the box of appealing to the company’s home audience in France as well as having wider international resonance. “Sean Connery is definitely universal while Stéphanie’s connection to the subject gives it a good anchor in France. That’s a perfect example of something that can speak across audiences,” she says, talking to Deadline just days after the announcement of her appointment. Career highlights & international mission The Canadian French documentary veteran has been working as a producer with CAPA since 2017. Documentary feature credits across her 20-year career include Su Rynard’s 2015 work The Messenger , exploring environmental threats to songbirds around the world, which she co-wrote, produced and edited. It premiered at Canada’s Hot Docs festival and was then acquired by Kino Lorber for the U.S. Under the CAPA umbrella, she was a producer on Ron Chapman’s Revival69: The Concert That Rocked the World, as well as Anastasia Trofimova’s Russians at War , which world premiered at the Venice Film Festival in 2024. More recent credits include the 2025 natural history two-parter 13 Hours to Survive , about how sea creatures tackle the challenge of being left high and dry by the tide, which played on Arte and Blue Ant Studio’s Love Nature platform; 2025 six-part, docu-series Marie Antoinette Confidential , coproduced with Banijay Studios France for Canal Plus, and TV docu-movie Tardigrade, the Indestructible Animal , which she also co-wrote. “I’ve been a producer with CAPA for a few years and was an independent producer previously, both in Canada and in France, so I have built up a big network for making international coproductions… the main reasons that they’ve given me this job is to push the international angle,” says Blake of her new role. “CAPA is the largest documentary production company in France. It’s really well known, really well established and producing for all the platforms and all the channels,” she continues. Blake cites true-crime series From Rock Star to Killer, about rock singer Bertrand Cantat, who killed his partner actress Marie Trintignant in 2003, and 2025 docu-drama November 13, Sonia’s Choice as examples of recent CAPA productions that have moved the dial in France. “ From a Rock Star to a Killer was a Netflix series which did really, really well. It was definitely in the top 10 of Netflix documentary series,” she says of the first title, which was released on the platform on March 2025. The two-part November 13, Sonia’s Choice recounts the true story of a woman at the heart of the hunt for the culprits of the Paris terror attacks on November 13, 2015, who is now living in hiding. It was broadcast in a primetime slot by state broadcaster France Télévisions on November 13, 2025, as part of its programming to mark the 10th anniversary of the attacks in which terrorists killed 130 people and injured many more across the French capital. “It was really interesting because it was an innovative hybrid film.” Blake says of the docu-drama, directed by David André and starring Carima Amarouche in the titular role. “Docu-drama is definitively one of the interesting areas we want to do more in. They’re working really well right now.” Blake believes strongly that the CAPA has the content, no-how and connections to expand its international footprint. “I think that the quality of the CAPA programming is something that could travel even more than it does now, and that’s something that I really, really want to make happen,” she says, adding that working with international partners is also becoming a necessity. “It’s something we all have to do right now when the industry is so difficult. We have to really, really look for those international partnerships and those ‘sneaky’ ways of financing things. You also need a sense of what’s out there, what the trends are, which is something I have, because I travel to all these markets quite a bit.” Alongside Sean Connery: The Untold Story, other upcoming CAPA productions that Blake feels have strong international potential include Compost . Being developed as a hybrid for the French market, it delves into the ecosystem and “drama” of a compost heap, exploring its inhabitants and the roles they play in breaking down food leftovers and garden refuse. “I have a long-standing experience in science, the environment and the natural world and of course that’s something that lends itself to international,” says Blake, citing titles such as 13 Hours to Survive. “I am currently working on a film, which is going to be primetime feature documentary for France Télévisions. The entire thing is going to be filmed in a compost heap… it will version and adapt very easily to other markets because composting, technically speaking, is something everyone can do,” she says. “It’s literally about the drama that happens inside a compost heap. Imagine the wooden boxes at the end of gardens, you open them up and it’s absolutely fascinating. It’s like a jungle in there with these tiny, tiny creatures. In the French version, the compost heap is in the back garden of a fictional family to give a human side to it, but the natural history part of the film can travel anywhere.” In the backdrop, Blake acknowledges it is a complex time for the documentary sector, with the genre making waves on the festival and awards circuit at the same as it faces funding squeezes. “There have been different waves. There was a contraction of the North American documentary market a few years ago that seems to have settled in the sense we know where we’re at right now. But recently, we’re seeing more and more crisis within public broadcasters in Europe. We’re definitely feeling that in France, but I think that’s happening all over,” she says. In spite of the challenges, Blake remains confident in the genre. “People are always looking for keys to decrypt the world, and the world is just getting scarier and more confusing, so I think there’s always going to be an interest in documentary.” 150 Tech Roles Set To Go; TV & Radio Network Closures Expected Next Week Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked; CNN Credentials Restored Key Asian Markets Set For $15B Content Spend In 2026 – Study HBO’s Bloys, Par’s Cheeks Fuel Merger Intrigue With Joint Appearance At ‘War’ Premiere Read More About: Comments

title: Anthony Kim Documentary From ‘Cocaine Quarterback’ Director Set at Propagate Content (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 24, 2026 5:00am Anthony Kim Jordan Bank/Getty Images An Anthony Kim documentary film from Jody McVeigh-Schultz ( Cocaine Quarterback: Signal-Caller for the Cartel , Spy High ) is in the works at Propagate Content , The Hollywood Reporter has learned. And if you do not know who Kim is, well, his story is very much deserving of the… honor? Kim was a golf prodigy and rising star until a 2012 achilles injury derailed not just his career, but his life. title: The Guardian To Offer ‘NAZA’ For Free On Website After Theatrical Run & Is Exploring Ways To Show Doc In Israel & Palestinian Territories
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie The Guardian To Offer ‘NAZA’ For Free On Website After Theatrical Run & Is Exploring Ways To Show Doc In Israel & Palestinian Territories ‘Maserati: The Brothers’ Actress Maya Talem Signs With MAD Celebrity ‘Ray Gunn’ Trailer: Netflix Adds Limited Theatrical Release For Brad Bird’s Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson-Voiced Animated Sci-Fi View All September 24, 2026 3:34am Filmmaker Yuval Abraham (right) interviews a source in 'NAZA' The Guardian/JW Films The Guardian and mk2 films have announced global release plans for Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor ’s bombshell documentary NAZA . The partners said that The Guardian-produced documentary will be released theatrically from September 28 onwards in more than 50 territories, having secured theatrical distributors in 56 territories since its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival on September 10, where it went on to win the Special Jury Prize. In an unprecedented move, The Guardian will make NAZA available for global audiences for free on its website, after the theatrical run later this fall. The partners said the move was due to the “worldwide interest” in the documentary as well as The Guardian’s “commitment to fearless, independent journalism”. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'On Standby' Renewed For Season 2 At Israel's Yes News 'Thirteen In Gaza' Trailer: Father & Daughter Tale Shot In Devastated Palestinian Territory Won NETPAC Award At TIFF The investigative documentary, exposing the Israeli military ‘s calculated targeting of civilians in Gaza in missile strikes through the testimony of intelligence personnel and soldiers involved in the killing, has caused a sensation since its Venice debut. It landed a record 25-minute ovation its Venice premiere Film , but has since been attacked by Israeli politicians including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has threatened to strip the directors of their Israeli citizenship even though he has no power to do this under the country’s laws. The Guardian and mk2 said the film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel , and they will be exploring other ways to enable the film to be seen in the occupied Palestinian territories. They added that, as previously announced, the film will receive its North American premiere on 26 September at New York Film Festival, and will open in U.S. theaters on September 30, launching exclusively at the IFC Center in New York City. It will expand to Los Angeles and other key markets on October 9, ahead of a national roll out in the weeks to follow. NAZA is produced by The Guardian and James Wilson (JW Films); and executive produced by Oscar-winning filmmaker Jonathan Glazer. The documentary builds on a series of revelations first published by the Guardian, +972 Magazine, a Israeli-Palestinian publication, and Hebrew-language outlet, Local Call between 2023-2025, including groundbreaking investigations into how Israel uses AI to identify targets in Gaza. It follows Abraham and Szor’s No Other Land , winner of the Best Documentary Academy Award in 2025. Co-directed with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, it documented Israeli army-backed efforts to erase the West Bank Palestinian villages of Masafer Yatta, while painting a wider picture of Israeli occupation. “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” said Abraham and Szor in a joint statement as the NAZA release plans were unveiled. “The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon.” Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers, added: “ NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years, but it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world.” “The initial response from those who’ve seen it shows audiences are engaging deeply with the urgent questions the film raises. We’re working with MK2 and international partners to bring the film to global audiences as soon as possible.” The 56 territories sold by Paris-based mk2 film, which boarded international sales on the documentary ahead of its Venice premiere, include France, UK, Italy, Spain, Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Greece, Portugal, Poland, Lithuania, Romania, Bulgaria, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Thailand, Canada, Brazil, Turkey, Central America, and the Middle East. 150 Tech Roles Set To Go; TV & Radio Network Closures Expected Next Week Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked; CNN Credentials Restored Key Asian Markets Set For $15B Content Spend In 2026 – Study HBO’s Bloys, Par’s Cheeks Fuel Merger Intrigue With Joint Appearance At ‘War’ Premiere Read More About: Comments

title: Streaming & Local Film Propel Major Asian Markets To $15B Content Spend This Year – MPA
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Streaming & Local Film Propel Major Asian Markets To $15B Content Spend This Year – MPA Samsung TV Plus Strikes Creator Channel Deals With Fearne Cotton & More; Expand Mark Rober Reach Independent Talent Group Buys Into Sports Agency Tongue Tied Management View All September 24, 2026 2:03am 'Paatal Lok' Prime Video Streaming and local film are set to send spend on content in seven major Asian markets over the $15B mark this year, according to a study. Media Partners Asia (MPA) reports that content investment will rise from $14.8B in 2025 to $15.1B this year and on to $15.4B in 2031. While TV currently accounting for 60% of the spend, followed by online video at 30% and film at 10%, MPA’s ‘Asia Video Content Dynamics 2026’ report noted “virtually all incremental growth comes from streaming and film as television budgets decline.” Related Stories News Korean Bestselling Thriller 'The Kidnapping Day' Set For Arabic-Language Movie Adaptation News Audiences Flocking To Anime On Netflix At 10 Times The Rate Of Other Genres, Report Reveals The report assessed spend in India , Indonesia , Korea , Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam , with key findings being that while Asian video industries command large audiences and have valuable brands, this is not always “converting into attractive financial returns” and many “established media companies” are trading “well below equity book value.” MPA is predicting those that spend wisely, rationalize costs and protect “genuine content advantages” will “increasingly separate” those that don’t. Watch on Deadline Within the $14.8B figure from 2025, Korea accounts for $6.9B, with India second at $5B, which is approximately 80% of the total. MPA noted streaming has overtaken TV in India with online video accounting for 46% of content investment in 2025, compared to 42% in television. Indian audiences streamed 420 billion hours last year, with JioHotstar leading the way with a 58% of the premium VOD viewing. Sports is driving demand, with JioHotstar experiencing a boost in reach during the IPL cricket season. In Korea, Netflix leads the way with domestic streamer TVING a clear second, while Indonesia’s Vidio, which has been profitable since the fourth quarter of last year, leading that market with six million paying subs. TVING’s extensive baseball rights helped expand its subs base from 5.3 million to 6.5 million, according to MPA. Local film represents “the region’s clearest growth opportunity,” MPA added. This was evidenced by Vietnam’s box office rising 20% to $213M in 2025 with local titles accounting for 69%. There were similar figures in Indonesia, while India posted a record box office total of $1.41B, and local titles were attributed for a “substantial theatrical recovery” in Korea this year. TV advertising, on the other hand, fell, with MPA suggesting “several television industries still carry more legacy capacity than their advertising economics can support.” Stephen Laslocky, Vice President, MPA, said: “Asia’s video industries are not short of audiences or creative capability. They are short of structures that convert both into sustainable returns. As the margin for error narrows, management quality will become decisive. Companies that rationalise legacy costs through restructuring and the adoption of new technologies such as AI, collaborate where independent investment no longer makes sense and protect the content that gives viewers a reason to stay will increasingly outperform, and the valuation gap between winners and losers will widen.” Another MPA analyst Myat Pan Phyu (May), added: “The viewership data shows demand is intact. Premium VOD engagement continues to grow across India, Korea and Southeast Asia, streaming now leads content investment in India, and local stories are winning at the box office from Hanoi to Jakarta and Mumbai. This is a story of reallocation rather than retreat as capital moves toward streaming and local film, where both audiences and returns are growing.” 150 Tech Roles Set To Go; TV & Radio Network Closures Expected Next Week Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked; CNN Credentials Restored Key Asian Markets Set For $15B Content Spend In 2026 – Study HBO’s Bloys, Par’s Cheeks Fuel Merger Intrigue With Joint Appearance At ‘War’ Premiere Read More About: Comments

title: ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Director Claire Scanlon Talks “Pressure” Of Chapter 16 Scene, “Dynamic” Captured With First Kiss & More
full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Director Claire Scanlon Talks “Pressure” Of Chapter 16 Scene, “Dynamic” Captured With First Kiss & More All The Songs In ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Film Adaptation: Gracie Abrams To Haim Streamer Subscription Prices And Tiers – Everything To Know As Costs Rise And Ads Abound View All September 23, 2026 2:26pm Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman in 'The Love Hypothesis' Prime Video SPOILER ALERT: This piece spoils the entirety of The Love Hypothesis movie now streaming on Prime Video . Editor’s Note: Trigger Warning – The following contains mention of sexual harassment. Help is available at the National Sexual Assault Hotline: 1-800-656-4673. The order of several pivotal scenes in Ali Hazelwood’s The Love Hypothesis was switched up for the film adaptation of the bestselling romance novel, which is directed by Claire Scanlon and stars Tom Bateman and Lili Reinhart. The Prime Video film centers on a fake dating ploy that benefits both parties — Olive (Reinhart) convinces her best friend Anh (Rachel Marsh) that Anh should shoot her shot with their mutual crush Jeremy (Nicholas Duvernay), and Dr. Adam Carlsen (Bateman) makes his higher-ups aware that he’s in a serious relationship and in no way planning to leave Stanford University, which has funded much of his research but pulled the plug based on rumors he might depart. What starts out as a simple business arrangement between Olive and Adam develops into real romance, which faces obstacles when a certain Dr. Tom Benton (Arty Froushan) comes to town. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Books All The Songs In ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Film Adaptation: Gracie Abrams To Haim News Everything We Know About ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Movie So Far The very important Chapter 16 sex scene between Olive and Adam was moved up in the film, and Scanlon already felt the “pressure” to get that one right alone. Luckily a test audience of 40% book readers and fans gave the green light. “When we started, there was just a quick paragraph of the sex scene, and then I read the book, and [said to] Sarah Rothschild, who wrote a great adaptation, ‘I think we need to build out that sex scene.’ Then I went on TikTok and I saw everyone [saying] ‘chapter 16, chapter 16.’ I was like, ‘Oh my goodness, this has to be more,’” Scanlon told Deadline. “Translating the book, which is over a chapter, to the screen — you can’t do that long with a sex scene. That would be not right. But just making sure that you got it tonally is always going to be tricky because everyone’s got their own internal dialogue and their own imagination of what it all looks like. We were ready for all the criticism, and then there wasn’t any.” To back up, a chaotic kiss with Carlsen initiated by Olive sets the fake-dating scheme of The Love Hypothesis into motion. Olive panics and smooches the first man she sees — who happens to be the notorious Doctor Evil — to throw Anh off the scent late one Saturday night in the lab. This snowballs into a whiplash of planned PDA and falling in love between the scientists. “We shot the first kiss on the first week. I wanted to make sure we got that dynamic established. And when we got that scene, I was like, ‘We have a movie’ because you just get all of it, watching it, trying to re-create the book cover in the actual scene. Paying homage to the book cover, and just in general, trying to get the tone of that scene, all the elements that were going into it. Anh’s coming up the stairs, [Olive]’s running this way. He’s like, “What?” Scanlon said. “Then he’s pissed because when you think about it from his point of view, he hasn’t been touched for years by anyone. Everyone’s so scared of him. That fact that someone smacked a kiss on him and then immediately rejects him, like that’s gotta suck, you know?” Carlsen quips about filing a Title IX complaint because Olive technically doesn’t wait for him to give consent before she kisses him. Another key moment that brings Title IX into the picture was shuffled to occur after the Chapter 16 scene, compared to book order: At the Society for Biological Development Conference, Carlsen’s colleague and seemingly close friend Benton, whose research aligns with Olive’s pancreatic cancer work, offers her a position on his lab bench at Harvard to continue conducting her experiments. But rather than base it off of Olive’s merit alone, he lays down the ultimatum that Olive must sleep with him in order to use his lab and equipment.

title: Peter Byrne Dies: Naked Eyes Singer Who Scored ’80s Hits ‘Always Something There to Remind Me’ & ‘Promises, Promises’ Was 74
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Peter Byrne Dies: Naked Eyes Singer Who Scored ’80s Hits ‘Always Something There to Remind Me’ & ‘Promises, Promises’ Was 74 Dick Guttman Dies: Longtime Hollywood Publicist To Barbra Streisand, Clint Eastwood, Paul Newman, Gary Cooper & Many More Was 93 Rachel Dratch & Jeff Hiller Join Encores’ ‘You’re A Good Man, Charlie Brown’; Gershwins’ ‘Let ’Em Eat Cake’ Added To Season View All September 23, 2026 2:55pm Pete Byrne of the Naked Eyes Getty Peter Byrne , the singer and songwriter for the band Naked Eyes who scored 1980s hits with “Always Something There to Remind Me” and “Promises, Promises,” died peacefully in Los Angeles, California, on Monday, September 14, after a brief illness. He was 74. His death was announced on the band’s official website . One of the most popular, if fleeting, British New Wave bands of MTV’s golden era, Naked Eyes was founded in 1982 by Byrne and keyboardist Rob Fisher, who had been college friends in their native Bath, England, and had performed together in a band called Neon from 1979 to 1982. (That band also included Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal, who would go on to form Tears for Fears.) Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Duncan Sheik Dies: “Barely Breathing” Singer-Songwriter & ‘Spring Awakening’ Composer Was 56 Within two years Naked Eyes had scored four Top 40 hits on Billboard’s Hot 100. The highest charting was “Always Something There to Remind Me” which peaked at #8 during the summer of 1983. A cover of the 1963 song written by Burt Bacharach and Hal David for Dionne Warwick, the Byrne-Fisher demo of “Always Something There to Remind Me” was strong enough to convince EMI Records to sign the duo that would become Naked Eyes. The band had three subsequent top 40 hits, the most successful of which was “Promises, Promises,” written by Byrne and Fisher and not to be confused with the Bacharach-David song of the same title that was a hit for Warwick. Both songs were included on the band’s debut 1983 album Burning Bridges , as was a third, less successful single “When the Lights Go Out.” DEADLINE RELATED VIDEO: The band’s second album, 1984’s Fuel For The Fire , featured a modest hit “(What) In the Name of Love,” but failed to match the success of the debut album, prompting Naked Eyes to disband (the group never toured). Fisher died in 1999 at the age of 42 following cancer surgery. Born June 9, 1952, in Bath, Byrne continued writing, recording and touring following Fisher’s death, releasing the solo album The Real Illusion in 2001 under Pete Byrne, followed by two albums under the Naked Eyes name: Fumbling with the Covers in 2007 and Disguise the Limit in 2021. A remaster of the original Naked Eyes self-titled album was release in 2025. In 2008 Byrne’s Naked Eyes took part in the U.S. “Regeneration” tour with Belinda Carlisle, ABC and the Human League, and in 2024 joined a similarly ’80s themed tour of the U.S. and Canada with Wang Chung, Men Without Hats and The Motels. Outside of Naked Eyes, Byrne’s work included providing backing vocals on Stevie Wonder’s 1985 hit “Part-Time Lover,” as well as songwriting for film and television. He wrote the song “I Am The Cute One” in 1993 for the Olsen Twins. Byrne is survived by his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve; children Merlin, Dylan, and Chloe; and ex-wife Elena. A private service will be held for the family. title: Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek Blames Bob Iger For Ouster In New Memoir
full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek Blames Bob Iger For Ouster In New Memoir Paramount Eyes Elon Musk For Investment As WBD Deal Nears Finish Line – Report Disney Hikes Price Of Disney+ And Hulu Streaming Plans View All September 23, 2026 3:29pm Bob Chapek Laurent Viteur/Getty Images; Simon & Schuster Bob Chapek , fired as Disney CEO in 2022 after less than three years, lays the blame for his ouster squarely on Bob Iger in an upcoming memoir, according to the New York Times, which obtained a copy. Behind the Castle Walls: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth comes out Sept. 29 from Gallery Books, a division of Simon & Schuster. Related Stories Executives Disney Shocker! Bob Iger Back As CEO, Bob Chapek Out Executives Did Someone Save Disney’s Life Last Night? Behind Bob Iger’s Stunning CEO Return & What’s Next For Media Giant “My abrupt dismissal hurt my reputation, leaving those close to me, outsiders and some within the kingdom trying to figure out what I did wrong,” Chapek writes. “The answer, again, is nothing.” Instead, he claims that Iger, who had handpicked him for the job, relentlessly and intentionally sabotaged him. Chapek’s belief on that front is no secret but he lays out his thoughts and defends his tenure publicly at length for the first time in the book. He calls himself a disrupter and writes, “I didn’t get a chance to finish what I started.” Watch on Deadline Iger resigned abruptly as Disney CEO in February of 2020 after an epic run but remained as executive chairman for two years, retaining control over creative endeavors at the company and reporting directly to the board of directors. Chapek reported to both the board, and to Iger. The two clashed. Chapek suggests that Iger believed he could reclaim the job whenever he wanted, the NYT says. Describing Iger’s exit from Disney, Chapek wrote, “I have been told by several high-ranking people both in government and private business that in their opinions, the real reason he left the company so abruptly was his anticipation of the arrival of Covid.” Disney declined to comment. The company has denied the pandemic had anything to do with Iger’s exit. Iger has said he wanted to wind down after a successful run. He felt at the time that Chapek was the right person for the job. “I had been CEO for about 15 years. I started the company in 1974 at ABC. I had been around a long time. There were plenty of things in the world that I was interested in that I either wanted to do or wanted to learn more about. I had not really had a day off in I don’t even remember,” Iger told a NYT DealBook conference in 2023 about his departure. He said he was “disappointed in what I was seeing, both during the transition period when I was still there and while I was out. But I really worked hard at distancing myself from it because one, I couldn’t do anything about. It in a way, it wasn’t my business at all, really. It was his business to run.” Soon after he started as CEO, Chapek was being pilloried on several fronts including management decisions that vexed key executives, and a public fight with star Scarlett Johansson that alienated talent. The company’s response to legislation (dubbed the ‘Don’t Say Gay’ bill) in Florida angered both Disney employees and Gov. Ron DeSantis. His ouster came shortly after Disney reported a greater than expected $1.5 billion streaming loss for its latest quarter. Chapek’s apparent rubber stamp by the Disney board, followed by his rocky tenure, was used as ammunition by activist investor Nelson Peltz in a bruising proxy fight with the Mouse House. title: As YouTube Remains Streaming’s Alpha Dog, It’s Adding Even More Unlikely New TV Tricks
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Barry Diller Drops Bid To Acquire Full Control Of MGM Resorts As YouTube Remains Streaming’s Alpha Dog, It’s Adding Even More Unlikely New TV Tricks As Living Room Viewing Booms, YouTube Debuts Live Dubbing, Shorts Series And Raft Of Other Features View All September 23, 2026 4:29pm Neal Mohan at YouTube Brandcast in 2026 Noam Galai/Getty Images for YouTube It’s been clear for a while that YouTube ‘s biggest screen in terms of viewing is the TV – but don’t expect the tech giant to just sit back on the couch. On the contrary, it is embracing the idea of adding more and more counter-intuitive features to the living room experience. At its annual Made on YouTube event Wednesday, the company unveiled nearly three dozen new features for creators, viewers and brands, the latest of what CEO Neal Mohan said were 3,000 new product updates in 2026 to date. Viewers on TVs can now post comments; view “posts” (still images and texts posted to channels by creators); and watch series on YouTube Shorts . Related Stories News Disney Hikes Price Of Disney+ And Hulu Streaming Plans News As Living Room Viewing Booms, YouTube Debuts Live Dubbing, Shorts Series And Raft Of Other Features These interactive elements are a key reason why YouTube has topped the Nielsen charts for three years straight with, as of July, 14.2% of all viewing via a TV in the U.S., executives say. (Of course, being available for free doesn’t hurt either.) Watch on Deadline “Consumption is moving away from being passive, and people want to be engaged,” Kurt Wilms, senior director of product management, YouTube on TV, told reporters after the New York event. Asked to elaborate, he clarified, “I wouldn’t call it passive. I would call it, like, lean back . I’m watching it. Something maybe happens in the show. And then I’m like, ‘Oh, well, I want to read the comments, or I want to leave a comment myself, or, wait, what did she just talk about a different video? I wanna go to her channel and see.’ So now, instantly I become a leaned-in viewer. And so I think it flows, ebbs and flows between two. We don’t think of them as a hard line.” Though its presence on landscape televisions seems counterintuitive, Shorts has been a runaway hit in the living room, with viewers watching more than 2 billion hours of its programming on TVs each month. Even inside the company, the reaction to the notion of adapting features from the mobile and web experience is often, “Is this meant for the TV?” Wilms said. “But we’re hearing viewers ask for it and creators ask for it.” The rollout of expanded capabilities is rooted in a mission to preserve the DNA of the first iteration of the site, which launched in 2005. (The first comment posted on “Me at the Zoo,” the first video ever uploaded, the company breezily noted on Wednesday, was a succinct “Lol.”) “We didn’t want it to feel broken,” Wilms said of the app when it is viewed on a TV. Although Shorts seems like a left-field stunner, in retrospect its success made perfect sense. “The first thing everyone was telling me about Shorts on the TV is there was no good way to watch this content with friends or family,” Wilms said. “The TV unlocked communal viewing for Shorts in a way that just wasn’t possible before.” The strategy of “bringing all these content formats that you might not think would resonate with viewers on the TV” has been a particular focus over the past two years, Wilms said, citing gaming videos, podcasts and shorts. “We saw it again actually around the same time with video comments,” he recalled. Viewers told the company, “‘I want to read the comments on TV,’ and we were thinking, ‘Really?! You want to read the comments on the TV?!'” While YouTube has not put numbers to it, Wilms estimated that the amount of viewers reading comments on TVs rivals the number doing so on the web. Similar to Shorts and comments, the Posts functionality resulted from consumer and partner research. “It’s all born out of creator and viewer feedback,” he said. “And we’ve seen time and time again when we bring [features] to the big screen, they’re successful.” Rather than bucketing viewers according to those who lean back and those who interact, Wilms says the company’s research shows a more blended experience. “One of the things when we talk to viewers that we hear about a lot is, we call it modes – like, a viewer is in a mode ,” Wilms said. “It might be, at night you want to use YouTube on your television as your home stereo and use it for music. Another mode might be you’re with your family and your kids, and you want to use YouTube as a way to watch with them. And so another mode that we’ve heard about is, ‘Oh, I don’t know totally what I want to watch, but I want to sit down and kind of get some quick bites, and so I go into this Shorts mode.” Enter microdramas, the booming sector that has spawned a host of startup studios along with optimism that the major component of the Asian entertainment ecosystem will gain similar adoption elsewhere. Microdramas “have been incredibly successful on YouTube,” Wilms said. “There are more than 6.5 billion views of this content on YouTube already this year. On TV screens specifically, microdramas are growing 90% year over year.” Execs see more upside ahead. “Microdramas in particular, they’re fast paced, they’re action packed, they’re quick, and so in the industry as a whole, I think viewers are resonating to this type of content, so I assume it’s gonna continue to grow,” Wilms added. Overall, we see a lot of success of bite-sized content that could be personalized to your taste. …. People are seeing it as a place to spend breaks in their day.” 150 Tech Roles Set To Go; TV & Radio Network Closures Expected Next Week Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked; CNN Credentials Restored Key Asian Markets Set For $15B Content Spend In 2026 – Study HBO’s Bloys, Par’s Cheeks Fuel Merger Intrigue With Joint Appearance At ‘War’ Premiere Read More About: Comments

Related Stories News Paramount Settlement Terms Laid Out By CA AG Rob Bonta, Who Says Deal Is “Not A Blessing” Of WBD Merger News David Ellison Hopes To Close Paramount-WBD Deal “In Approximately Two Weeks” As He Hails Legal Settlement In Company Memo “The only antitrust related provisions in the States’ settlement require that Paramount honor its already-stated commitments to maintain and grow its movie and TV businesses.” The DOJ signed off on the $111 billion merger in June, with no concessions from Paramount of requirements of divestitures. Merger opponents criticized the DOJ’s review as insufficient amid Paramount’s wooing of the Trump administration, and the next month a dozen state attorneys general sued to halt the transaction. Watch on Deadline But a settlement was announced Monday that includes a set of behavioral conditions to last for five years, including a commitment by Paramount to release 30 films for the first and second years, and 32 films for the third, fourth and fifth years. The consent decree also includes a theatrical release window of at least 45 days. Paramount CEO David Ellison had previously stated he would commit to such windows and to the 30-movies-per-year releases. Woodward said in his statement, “Consumers benefit when transactions close quickly after federal enforcers have concluded a substantive review. Under President Trump’s leadership, DOJ will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy.” At a press conference Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta , who led the 12 states in the litigation, repeatedly said the settlement would be an “enforceable commitment,” including that it would “significantly increase domestic production in the United States, and necessarily production right here in L.A., in Hollywood.” Among other things, he said, Paramount also would spend $300 million more each year in domestic film production, while agreeing to conduct Paramount and Warner Bros cable channel negotiations independently. The settlement also includes an independent monitor to oversee compliance, Bonta’s team noted. Bonta had previously indicated that only a structural remedy — like a commitment to divest assets — would suffice when it came to a settlement. The consent decree does contain requirements to sell off Miramax and selected cable channels if there are breaches of the settlement terms. Just last week, before the settlement was reached, the DOJ sided with Paramount in its motion to require that the state AGs put up a $1.88 billion bond as the litigation dragged on. The trial had been scheduled for March, but Paramount faced having to pay a $7 million-per-day ticking fee to Warner Bros. Discovery for each day that the merger didn’t close after September 30. The Chairman and CEO of HBO and Max Content is a fixture at all of the streamer’s events, so him attending the red-carpet premiere of the new drama series War in New York on Tuesday night was not a surprise. His plus-one, George Cheeks , was. Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Cheeks is Chairman of TV Media for Paramount , a company in the final stages of acquiring HBO parent Warner Bros Discovery. Bloys and Cheeks’ joint appearance was arranged weeks ago, sources said, with Bloys inviting his friend to a premiere of a buzzy new show. They kept the affair relatively private by not posing for photos together. Still, the sight of top Paramount and WBD TV executives together stirred a lot of buzz at the event, coming just a day after a settlement in 12 state attorneys general’s antitrust lawsuit was announced, paving the way for the Paramount-WBD merger to close in the next two weeks after months of uncertainty. Watch on Deadline Bloys similarly got tongues wagging in March when he was spotted lunching with Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos just a couple of weeks after Netflix had walked away from its proposed merger of WBD following the late $111 billion bid by Paramount. The HBO boss’ social engagements are being closely scrutinized because what he will do next is one of the most intriguing questions surrounding the Paramount-WBD merger. Paramount CEO David Ellison and Sarandos have both spoken highly of Bloys, who is coming off another strong Emmy season at HBO where he is under contract through 2027. Bloys is expected to be a key part of Ellison’s plans for the combined Paramount-WBD. It is the way streaming leadership is structured with the planned merger of Paramount+ and HBO Max that would determine whether Bloys and Paramount Chair of Direct to Consumer Cindy Holland both stay or one of them leaves as it’s likely neither would report to the other. Current speculation is that Bloys would stay on, with Netflix chatter remaining in the background. Cheeks, the only Paramount co-CEO to continue after the company’s 2025 acquisition by Skydance, is part of Ellison’s senior management team and is expected to carry on, with his role possibly adjusted post-WBD merger. (Heading into the transaction, Cheeks oversees Paramount’s basic cable networks, while Channing Dungey, Chairman and CEO of the Warner Bros. Television Group and Warner Bros. Discovery’s US Networks, does the same for the WBD ones, raising questions whether the combined cable portfolio will be consolidated or remain split.) So, Cheeks’ visit to the War premiere may have been a precursor, similarly to then-Discovery CEO David Zaslav’s October 2021 attendance of the Season 3 premiere of HBO’s Succession alongside Bloys while the Discovery-WarnerMedia merger was still being finalized. The situation is a little different as Bloys and Cheeks are considered peers with their areas not expected to overlap if both stay on at Paramount, making their premiere date two potential co-workers hanging together. title: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives ‘Dynamic Duo’ & Untitled ‘Gremlins’ Head To Fall 2028 Amid Warner Bros Release Date Changes UTA Signs ‘Club Kid’ Star Reggie Absolom View All September 23, 2026 4:34pm Story Arc Paramount & Warner Bros water towers Getty Images UPDATED: A Zoom call on Wednesday with 500 senior Warner Bros staffers to discuss Paramount ‘s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by state attorneys general related to its merger with WBD did little to dissipate the gloomy, Mordor-like clouds over the Burbank lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference. The video call, which has been routine since Paramount won the $110 billion bid for Warner Bros Discovery, was led by WBD Studios Chief Operating Officer Simon Robinson, who is running point on the merger integration; Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar; WBD Chief Comms Officer Robert Gibbs; and HR boss Amy Girdwood . According to sources, the four conceded they didn’t have much visibility into Paramount’s plans for a newly combined company, but indicated that the anticipation is for the deal to close in about 10 days, in line with Paramount CEO David Ellison ‘s two-week timeframe he provided Monday. Related Stories News David Ellison Says “We Have Complete Clearance For This Merger” After Settlement With State AGs Over Paramount WBD News Post-Merger Paramount May Overdeliver On Settlement Terms With 36-Film 2027 Slate Amid Speculation About Duplication & WB Leadership The name and the leadership structure of the new company will likely be announced ahead of close, the executives reportedly said, though they weren’t clear as to when exactly that might be. We heard that Girdwood told leaders to take a moment to reflect on the great work accomplished during their tenures. Watch on Deadline “It feels like a scramble,” one source said. To say staffers were surprised by the AG settlement Monday doesn’t really cover it. “It was a big shock,” one person said. “If you were riding the roller coaster, you felt like things were not progressing.” Still, even if the settlement and its timing came as a surprise, the ultimate result seemed inevitable as WBD CEO David Zaslav has been hellbent on selling the studio. Ellison’s takeover of the cinematic institution founded by Albert, Harry, Sam and Jack Warner “was always bound to happen,” one insider exclaimed. Zaslav, who is likely to walk away with more than $600 million from the $110B merger, was not on today’s Zoom, we’re told. The Ellison-run Paramount has said that the Warner Bros acquisition will yield $6B in synergy savings, which don’t necessarily translate into job cuts, but rather by reducing inefficiencies in other structural areas (i.e., real estate portfolios, data servers). But Warner Bros staffers aren’t buying that. “We’ve been here before. We know what it looks like,” said one insider about the changeover in ownership of Warner Bros over the past decade. It was only four years ago that AT&T dumped WarnerMedia into the hands of Discovery. Myriad people inside Warner Bros are cynical about the capping of severances and the fact that only a few at the top are bound for a post-merger windfall. There’s also ire over the pausing of contract renewals due to the acquisition, as well as irritable infighting between departments about theatrical failures this year: No one WB title has cleared $100M at the domestic box office, with the highest-grossing movie stateside being Wuthering Heights at $84M. Home entertainment and data analytics divisions were none too happy about DC’s Supergirl tanking; with its $186M net production cost and a global box office gross of $126.3M, key staffers believe DC Studios chose the wrong comic book character to adapt. On the immediate horizon as the Paramount-Warner Bros marriage comes together is Digger, the $125M political satire starring Tom Cruise, directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu and produced by Legendary. It opens on October 2. While domestic debut prospects are at around $20M, Warners is hoping to get past any sour headlines about box office-to-cost ratios on the film, much like it did on One Battle After Another, as the four-time Oscar-winning filmmaker’s Doctor Strangelove -like epic is being primed as an awards-season contender. It is a chip Paramount really doesn’t have on its year-end schedule. The new Paramount could also inherit another awards contender and its first billion-dollar-grossing title since Skydance took over the Melrose Ave lot with Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three. That opens on December 18. To date, the Denis Villeneuve franchise counts $1.12B at the global box office and eight Oscars. We’ve heard on the Paramount side that it’s still TBD in regards to how the merger will handle duplications in marketing and distribution. Warner Bros international distribution has more of a solid presence in offshore territory offices and staffers than Paramount, which needs to untangle itself from UIP. Paramount could find great muscle in Warners International distribution and marketing infrastructure. While we were told by Paramount sources that the plan isn’t to create two studios, it might be wise for Ellison to keep each respective marketing team at their respective labels if he wants each studio working to the top of their creative merits and box office strengths: former Warner Bros exec Josh Goldstine presiding over global marketing and distribution at Paramount, and the team he built at Warners — Dana Nussbaum and Christian Davin in global marketing along with Creative Advertising EVP John Stanford–exactly over at Warners. Marketing and distribution rolls up and reports into the motion picture heads. During Warner Bros’ $4.38B grossing 2025, the trio of Nussbaum, Davin, and Stanford achieved great innovative marketing efficiencies, we’re told, and yes, those 11 Oscars for the Burbank, CA lot. There’s also a thick fog around those staffers who were bound to decamp from Warner Bros proper in the previously planned Gunnar Wiedenfels-led Global Networks spinoff. Yes, Warner Bros staffers are already putting themselves out there for other jobs. Some of them have already found new gigs: Former EVP Comms Katie Martin Kelly, prized by Warner Bros Motion Picture group co-heads Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, high-tailed it for Netflix as her contract ended, rather than wait for the Russian roulette the new conglomerate could bring. Former HBO Max EVP Originals Marketing Pia Barlow found a new job at Amazon MGM Studios as their Series Marketing VP, a gig that triggered WBD to sue for poaching. The merger closing will likely trigger more voluntary departures as many WBD executives had been waiting to cash out stock options post-transaction, no longer bound by contracts that typically provide a way out in case of change of ownership. “Since David Zaslav took control of Warner Bros, there’s just been thousands of jobs lost,” one former Turner publicist emphatically told us. “Those are jobs that the entertainment industry is never going to get back.” And therein lies the ultimate piercing wound for any Warners or Paramount employee in the danger zone: The fact that there are not a lot of jobs out there is a big deal. What’s more, adds a source, “People are very concerned about the survival of the Warner Bros brand.” Counters a senior ranking insider at the conglomerate: “There’s a feeling of relief from senior executives to junior staff about the possibilities that the new company can bring. They were very excited by David Ellison’s note.” For now, Paramount is inheriting at least 39 Warner Bros theatrical releases on the calendar dated between October 2 this year and the end of 2028. That output reps 56% of what will be a currently combined 70 features between the two studios. During the agita of Netflix and Paramount courting Warner Bros, the studio’s greenlighting of productions has been at a loud hum; assumptions were made by some that Warner Bros Motion Pictures would be in purgatory during merger talk time, and that filmmakers and reps would be wary of taking projects to them. That’s not really an option for content creators at a time when it’s a miracle for any major motion picture to get off the ground. Something to look forward to: While a Barbie sequel hasn’t been greenlit due to ongoing talks with top-tier talent including director Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, expect that to be one of the first orders of business for the new Ellison-owned Paramount-Warner Bros. Beams one optimistic Warner exec, “The new merger gives us the all the financial resources to compete on a level with the big streamers.” 150 Tech Roles Set To Go; TV & Radio Network Closures Expected Next Week Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked; CNN Credentials Restored Key Asian Markets Set For $15B Content Spend In 2026 – Study HBO’s Bloys, Par’s Cheeks Fuel Merger Intrigue With Joint Appearance At ‘War’ Premiere More from this Story Arc Paramount WB September 23, 2026 HBO’s Casey Bloys & Par’s George Cheeks Go To ‘War’ Together: Execs’ Joint Premiere Appearance Creates Intrigue With WBD Merger Closing September 22, 2026 Judge Sets Hearing On State AGs’ Settlement With Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery View All Story Arc Read More About: 4 Comments

De Heer’s 2022 film The Survival Of Kindness , which was selected for competition at the Berlinale, will screen in Tokyo as part of an Australia Spotlight, a special showcase of Australian cinema presented in cooperation with the Australian Embassy in Japan. Based in Tasmania, de Heer has a career spanning more than 40 years and widespread international acclaim, starting with Bad Boy Bubby (1993), which won the Special Jury Prize and FIPRESCI Prize at Venice. Other early career highlights include Dingo (1991) with Colin Friels and jazz legend Miles Davis; The Quiet Room (1996) and Dance Me To My Song (1998), both selected for Competition at Cannes. title: Meta Introduces New VR Glasses With Access To Content From YouTube, Prime Video, HBO Max, Disney+ & More

Meta VR Glasses will deliver cinema, TV and sports content in one device with access to Prime Video, YouTube, Peacock, HBO Max, and Paramount+, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, Tubi, the NBA, MLB, ESPN, MLB, NBC Sports, TNT Sports and UFC, some with virtual and 3D enhancements.
